He said: Mr. Speaker, the object of this bill is to restore a wholesome safeguard which was in the Criminal Code prior to 1919 with respect to sedition. We have no definition of sedition in our code. Although we have certain purported explanations or definitions of what seditious words are, what seditious libels are, or what seditious conspiracies are; they are definitions which do not define to any great extent. OCEAN SHIPPING RATES
subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED

speechtext: The House resumed, from March 17, the adjourned debate on the motion of Hon. T. A. Low (Minister of Trade and Commerce) to ratify and confirm a contract between His Majesty and Sir William Petersen providing for the establishment of a subsidized steamship line on the Atlantic, and government control of certain ocean rates, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Clark.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: OCEAN SHIPPING RATES
subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion
under debate reads as follows:
That to give the government of Canada control over certain ocean rates it is expedient to ratify and confirm the agreement between His Majesty and Sir William Petersen, K.C.B.E., as set out in the schedule to this resolution, and dated the eleventh day of December, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-four, and that in view of the provisions of said agreement giving the government control over such rates and of the services to be performed thereunder, the Governor in Council may authorize payment out of the consolidated revenue fund, to the said Sir William Petersen, K.C.B.E., of an annual amount of two hundred and seventy-five thousand pounds in the manner and for the period provided for in the said agreement.
Then follows the specific agreement. I read this so that the House, after being carried far over the waters of controversy, may get some glimpse of the port towards which we are sailing. I think it is important that we know what is before the House in its exact terms.
One would think from much of the debate that has preceded, and he would certainly think from the speech of the Prime Minister, that the motion before the House was to appoint a committee to inquire into the north Atlantic combine, and if possible, devise some method whereby the freight rates of that combine could be controlled. The House has been told that a desire to control is all the principle we are voting for; and those who favour control are told that the only thing to do is to support the resolution. Of course, those who are opposed to control and who like high rates are informed that they will be quite logical in opposing the resolution. If a government is to instruct the House- and if its word is to be the last on the subject-as to what principle it wishes to attach to a motion, then parliament might just as well become an appendage, a mere servile register of the administration's will. I think it is better for us to assume that we ourselves can read, and that we can understand the English language; and when we are asked to ratify a contract, common sense dictates to me that the principle which we are asked to affirm is the principle of that contract. If a government, on the introduction of any resolution or bill can say, "The principle of this resolution, this bill, is merely the public welfare, and those who support the public welfare must support this measure"-if a government can take such an attitude, then of course parliament will never have any question before it at all. An object to be gained is not necessarily a principle, it certainly is not a policy; a policy is the method proposed to reach the object. Now, it is true that a
Ocean Shipping Rates

government measure, merely because it passes in the form of a resolution or in the form of a second reading, need not finally pass unamended in detail; nor has anyone ever so contended. But every self-respecting government does insist that a government measure shall pass only with such amendments as do not vitally affect the measure itself. And when a government informs the House that it is not at all particular about its proposal, that all it wants is some way of reaching the goal, and that if the House will suggest some other method it will be gladly followed, then the government simply abdicates its duties, surrenders all its functions, and becomes nothing more nor less than surplusage in parliament.
The motion before us, is such that this argument applies with double force. The resolution preceding the bill asks us to affirm that it is expedient to ratify an agreement already entered into, signed and sealed, by the administration. The records of parliament will be searched in vain to disclose any case in which any government in our history, or in the history of the British parliament or of any dominion, ever suggested that an agreement signed and sealed by themselves, an agreement into which they had entered as fair between themselves and the other party, was subject to anything at the hands of parliament save acceptance or rejection. Indeed, this was the stand first taken by the Prime Minister; and in answer to, or rather in interruption of several speakers, he declared that what parliament had before it was the duty of deciding whether to reject or to approve of the contract which the resolution embodies. In so speaking he followed every precedent. But, as the difficulties of the situation loomed up, as the clouds gathered round his government, as he looked across at the gloomy faces of hon. gentlemen to my left, he proceeded by a slow curve to alter his position. He altered it first to the extent of saying that the agreement must pass; or, if the House considered that it could be amended, the government would take the amendments to Sir William Petersen and see whether he would agree to them. In the first place, this is not a very dignified attitude for any government to assume. Every citizen having made a contract feels that he should live up to it to the extent of his power. Having agreed that the terms of the contract are fair and reasonable, he does not like to submit to the humiliation of going back to the contractee and asking for a change. Well, what is true of a citizen in that regard should be far truer of a government. But this gov-
ernment, having declared its belief that the terms of the contract before us are fair and reasonable, is prepared to go back to Sir William Petersen and to say, "A committee of the House does not like this contract, so we are ready to kneel at your feet and beg of you to change its terms". This does not define fully the position which the Prime Minister took. He said further that if Sir William Petersen refused to consent to any change in the contract then it would be for the government to stand or fall by the agreement as it is. But again, the altered attitude did not seem to appeal to hon. gentlemen whose votes he was seeking very eagerly. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speak-man) following of course the statements of the Prime Minister, made it clear that he would not consider the government acting in good faith unless the committee was free to devise some plan of control without subsidies at all-a wholly different plan or principle from that embodied in the contract. And the Prime Minister then declared that all that anyone would be voting for who voted for the contract was the "principle" that he desired ocean rates to be controlled, adding that if the committee favoured some other method and suggested it, it would be for the government to come back to parliament and, as best it could, give expression by a new measure to what it believed to be the will of parliament. In a word, the Prime Minister has declared that the government is prepared to change its policy, to the left or to the right, provided it can save its precious existence.
At times when a resolution is proposed, the House, if the case is unimportant, frequently lets the resolution pass, reserving decision on the principle for the second reading of the bill. But when the resolution is challenged by amendment then the government's policy as embodied in that resolution is at stake; and from that fate no government can escape. And that is the position which the government is in at the present time. I read the motion in order to bring to hon. gentlemen an understanding of what is meant, and I close this phase of the subject by asking this question: If the principle of government control by subsidies, in accordance with the terms of this contract if indeed this contract itself is not now before us for decision, when is it going to be, or when can it ever be? I submit that question this moment to every member of the government, sitting in front. Will it be on the first reading of the bill? Will it be on the second reading? And let us remember that the second reading is the last prior to

Ocean Shipping Rates
the committee stage, prior to the establishment of the select committee. When the second reading of the bill is before the House the Prime Minister can say exactly the same thing: "Oh, all that you are voting for is to have a special committee, and you will be given a chance to devise policies to suit yourselves." He can say that with just the same force and effect as he says it now. In other words, if the position which the Prime Minister takes is to be accepted by the House, then the House can never decide at all on the merits of this contract, or of the definite policy it proposes.
Now, it is well to inquire just what the real situation is with which we are confronted. The Prime Minister spent a considerable portion of his address in reciting conditions and circumstances which, I think, all of us know to exist; and it will contribute to definiteness in this discussion, as well as to clearness of thinking, if we can proceed to agree on what appeared to be conclusions from a large portion of his speech.
We can agree in the first place that there is a North Atlantic Steamship Conference- or combine if you wish to call it such. Nobody has ever disputed it that I have heard. We can agree that such conference or combine fixes rates on the goods its members transport. I do not know of anyone who disputes that; its officers did not dispute it before the committee presided over by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster).

maintopic: OCEAN SHIPPING RATES
subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: I think it only fair to state that the officers of the lines denied that there was a conference, and the fact was only brought out with considerable difficulty.

maintopic: OCEAN SHIPPING RATES
subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
It will be left for the hon. gentleman to establish what he says. I have read the report and I did not read that statement. I do not think any hon. member of this House doubts for a minute that a conference exists to-day and has existed for many years, and that the rates on the commodities are fixed by conference, with one or two or three exceptions. The argument has convinced me that the grain rate is not fixed by the conference. There may be an extent to which flour and cattle rates were fixed by it or possibly are to-day,-that matter may be left in dispute, it is not material for the moment,-but that rates are fixed generally there is no dispute. It may be taken for granted also that rates have been very materially advanced since pre-war days, and that
the advance in those rates has had the effect of making difficult the export of goods; that it would be much better for Canadian industries if the rates were lower; and that possibly we would have some other Canadian industries if there were no rates at all. It can be taken for granted, as well, that repeated complaints have been made against those rates, back for six or eight years past,-yes, for longer than that,-and that those complaints are still kept up. All these things we acknowledge; it need not have taken three hours of declamation to establish them. I think we can agree further still, that the element of competition, to some degree is eliminated in respect of water-borne traffic. I do not think it is eliminated at all to the extent that it is eliminated in land transport, nor does any hon. member of this House think so. It is impossible in the present evolution of the industry to eliminate competition, save to a limited degree.
Yet, while we agree on all these things, we do not get very far towards enlightenment on the merits of this resolution; but once we agree on these things we dispose of at least three hours of the speech of the hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). Now I state that there is not the same competition as in earlier days on the water. I make this further affirmation for whatever hon. gentlemen accept it as worth-that when the ocean steamship business develops to the extent that regular liners are established, then it is essential that there be something in the nature of conference and fixing of rates for those lines. I wonder if there is any member of this House who really believes that in evolution of the ocean steamship business to the extent that regular sailings are established, just as regular despatch of trains is established on land, it is possible to continue, save by some system of conference and uniformity of rates. I do not think the Prime 4 p.m. Minister would say so. In a portion of his speech, towards the end, he clearly indicated the contrary. It cannot be done. If you do not have some such system, you are going to have each reaching out after the big fellow's traffic, giving rebates and advantages to obtain it-this is in evidence;-and thereby discriminations are produced which are far more serious than any discriminations complained of in this debate. The little fellow as a shipper will be virtually eliminated. This uniformity of rates established for the liner ensures to all equal treatment, to all shipments from all quarters no
Ocean Shipping Rates

matter whether those shipments be large or small. Further, when we have the line transport system established, as stated in the report of the American government commission, experience has proven that there is no middle road between peace and war, and the big liner company has such advantage over the smaller that the crushing out process is sure to be successful, with the consequent establishment of a monopoly, not only in rates but in service. The element of competition even in service is gone forever. These things follow if there is no conference system; and consequently the conference system is not necessarily an evil in itself.
I do not argue from all this that as the shipping business grows and as the system evolves and these conferences become essential with the incident fixing of rates which is the main purpose of the conference, I do not argue that such thing can go on indefinitely with no superimposed control. I believe that the principle is unsound, that you can leave control solely in a conference; for while to do so is less dangerous than to suffer the absence of higher control on land-for the reason that on land competition in rates is absolutely impossible-on sea there is some competition, some very substantial competition, because of the presence of a very vast number of tramps-still sea transport should be controlled. These tramps according to the finding of the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) in 1913, are not a great 'factor in competition in respect of goods which must have the liner service, which for the sake of regularity are practically dependent on the liner; but in respect of a great vast array of commodities the tramp competition is effective. Consequently we have not so soon arrived at the stage in the world's affairs when there is some supervision of ocean transport rates, the stage we have reached in respect of land transport rates. I admitted a moment ago that we had had in late years very material increases in ocean rates. The Prime Minister read at great length letters from shippers showing in respect of certain commodities rather startling percentages of increase. I do not doubt that some large percentages do obtain, but I might point out to
the Prime Minister that his mathematics in some cases are out. But this is aside from the point. The only way in which we can establish what the advance has been is by such a computation as takes all rates into account; the selecting of isolated rates on tooth picks or clothes pins, on some little commodity such as those and working it out to a percentage leads to no conclusion. You ask me what does a computation of the whole field of commodities show? I had produced to me just a few minutes ago a schedule prepared from the Index of Shipping Freights. This is the official index accepted I believe everywhere as authoritative on this question. The schedule takes the average of rates, 1898 to 1913, as the basis. That average is stated to be 100. One would have thought that evidence of this kind, which agrees very closely and accurately with the tables produced in the Economist are surely of more value than a plethora of miscellaneous letters which have been written at various times, mostly long ago, by different persons in the country about matters, the actual facts as to which may never have been investigated and the circumstances respecting which are now unknown. I stated a moment ago that as the conference system develops-and it has developed to a very considerable degree-it seems reasonable and essential that there be developed with it a supervising authority, an authority competent to control the disposition of the power now vested in the conference. It does not seem reasonable to my mind that an authority which does not represent all the people should be competent to dispose of the world's water freight, and I say that without any allegation that there has been discrimination or wrongdoing or extortion of any kind in respect of such disposition; but the principle seems 
wrong that there should go on uncontrolled an authority over these very vital matters in the hands of those whose interests are not in every way the interests of the whole people.
But when we get to that point, is not the next thing we have to decide, what necessarily must be the composition, what necessarily must foe the status of any body that is to have a chance in the world to exercise anything in the nature of control? Surely any single country has not such right-and because it has not the right it never can succeed in an attempt to exercise it. I ask hon. gentlemen to reflect, has Canada alone the right to control rates in and out between this country and Great Britain? If we have such a right, has not Great Britain the same right? And how can both of us have the right to separate control? Now I pause for a reply from any hon. gentleman in this House. Have we the right to control rates between here and Australia, or to dictate to Australia what shall be charged on goods shipped from that Dominion to Canada? Have

Ocean Shipping Rates
we the right to say to Great Britain, "On the goods sent by your citizens to this country only such and such shall be the freight rates and we are going to dictate those rates right here in the Capital of Canada?" Let us reverse the position; let us suppose that Great Britain had proposed that its government would control the rates on our wheat shipped from the shores of Canada to the British market, can any hon. gentleman imagine to himself the speech that the Prime Minister of this country would deliver in this House? Can anybody conceive the compaign which would be launched in this Dominion against "Downing street domination?" Well, if Great Britain has not that right, how then can we assert the right to control rates between here and that country? In a word, we are asserting something which inherently we do not and cannot possess, and even if we had some wise method established to exercise such right, the wisest you could get, our attempt would be bound to end in failure.
Now, what kind of a board, what is the smallest circumference or power a board must possess which could even attempt to handle this situation? I venture to suggest to the House, and it is embodied in our amendment as an affirmation, that you cannot do so with any body of narrower compass than a body on which are representatives of the whole empire. Even the Prime Minister in a portion of his address said it could not be effectively done until you had a body representative of all nations of the world. Well, possibly to a degree that is true. But the shipping of this whole empire is of so vast a magnitude that it cannot be boycotted, and the people of this whole empire have among themselves the inherent right, if they choose to exercise it, to control the shipping between the various ports of the empire. Therefore the first- step of any consequence at all that is not bound to end in disaster and collapse is to establish some such body on which the whole empire is represented. Every effort should be persisted in to bring this about. I do not say that when this is done it will be the last step in the development of a system of control, there may be one beyond, but that step has a chance, a good chance, of succeeding in so far at least as traffic is concerned -between the various ports of the British Empire. .
Hon. gentlemen opposite who entered into this agreement very hastily,-and some of whom I do the compliment to say are exceedingly sorry-tell us, "Oh we cannot get any body in which the whole empire is represented to take this matter in hand so we
have got to splurge ahead and do something, no matter whait it is, in order to attract attention, in order to stir our cousins up and have them see this thing has got to be attended to." Well, what have been the attempts? According to the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham), the first was started in 1910. He got a memorandum from Mr. Justice Mabee, then head of the railway commission. He forwarded that memorandum to the British government, and the British government made a reply. Now, I have the highest opinion of the late Mr. Justice Mabee, but I must express the fear that I cannot be lost in admiration of his memorandum. It proceeds on the hypothesis that ocean transport is as susceptible of control by one country as is land transportation within that country itself; it proceeds on the hypothesis that competition is just as surely gone from ocean transport as from land. Both of these hypotheses are manifestly and obviously false. I do not need to go further. The memorandum says also that in a few years-it was written in 1910-England would be importing 600,000,000 or 800,000,000 bushels of our wheat. Well, as to-day, fifteen years after, there are only about 43,000,000 people in Great Britain, and all they could possibly consume would be 280,000,000 bushels, I am at a loss to know what they would do with the other 400,000,000 bushels. In a word, the memorandum is not very thoroughly compiled. It was forwarded to Great Britain with an expression of hope that some central body representative of the empire would be created to take charge of this transport difficulty.
Evidently the Canadian government of the time forgot that the whole question had just been investigated by a commission on which the government itself had been represented, and that commission's finding was that control on the water, as compared with control on the land, was impracticable, that there were very, very great difficulties to be confronted which did not appear on land at all, and that especially a control which necessarily, if it operated, would put British shipping at a disadvantage with continental shipping was something which would not redound to the benefit of any part of the Empire. These things were pointed out by the British government. Well, they seem to me very sensible. I wonder how they appeal to other members of this House. Do not the representations made by the British government in its reply sound sane and just and right. There were undoubtedly further difficulties to be overcome, and the British government suggested that the matter be still further investigated with a view to seeing if
Ocean Shipping Rates

something could not be evolved to take care at least of the danger of discriminations. The Canadian government stopped right there. The Minister of Railways says the reason they stopped was that he knew when he was turned down, and anyway they knew the facts and needed no investigation. This was back in 1910 and such is the reason he gave the House for having gone no further. Well, if they knew the facts in 1910, why did they start to find them out again in 1923 and again in 1924? They started two investigations in the last two years.
The next step of importance taken-I am passing by the various inquiries at the hands of the British government-was an inquiry by the present hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton). He made an inquiry from the standpoint of Canada and returned with a report which, put in brief, was this: that he did not believe the principle of private control under the conference system could be allowed to continue undisturbed; that there should be some higher control; that otherwise, the conference would have power at its own will, to do injustice and injury to individual concerns. While he did not allege it had done so, he did, not believe it was in principle right that the power should be solely vested there, and he suggested a tribunal which was to seek to evolve a plan. He mentioned that- the Dominions Royal Commission then sitting was the proper body. This royal commission evidently took the matter in hand, and reported against the principle of private control and in favour of some system of united control on the part of the various parts of the empire. The war was on. Through the period of the war shipping was under the British government. In 1918 the representatives of Canada brought this matter forcibly to the attention of that government. The British government acquiesced to the extent of appointing what is known as the Imperial Shipping committee on which all portions of the empire are represented and to which certain definite powers were given. These did not include powers specifically to fix rates; those were withheld; but the committee was invited to investigate and report on all matters concerning discriminations, harbour facilities, and generally the betterment of communications between the various portions of the empire. Canada was not satisfied. Sir Robert Borden in the spring of 1919 prepared a memorandum in which he strongly urged that the powers of the shipping board be amplified and that Canada continue in its effort-and he invited the support of the other dominions as well-to have vested in this Imperial Shipping Board a

power of control. This was subsequently submitted to me, when I was Prime Minister, in a letter from Sir George Perley. Sir George Perley had been our representative on the Imperial Shipping Board. Considerable good work was done by that board. He found, however, that he was not possessed adequately of the information necessary in order to bring home to the commission the duty of reporting itself in favour of being given these powers, and he asked us to consider the wisdom of having someone specially delegated to present the case of Canada, in favour of the amplification of the duties of the Imperial Shipping Board. The government of the day decided that Dr. Magill of Winnipeg was capable to do that work. Dr. Magill, however, declined. The letter in which he declined is not before us, but there was such a letter. This was during the session of 1921. At the close of the session I went to England, and immediately on my return a general election was called. Six months, or almost that, intervened between the reply of Sir George Perley and the calling of the general election. The session of parliament and Imperial conference were on and progress was not made.
The next step was the appointment of the committee under the charge of the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster). This committee, however, was not appointed to investigate ocean freight rates at all; the reference to the committee contained no suggestion of such investigation. The reference was general, to look into the question of agricultural conditions. I make no complaint that the committee saw fit to give some attention to this subject; I am very glad it did. The committee made several reports, and now we are told that the government bases the policy it submits to parliament upon the report of that committee. Well, one would never dream so, if he reads the report itself. The report found that there was a combine and that the combine controlled rates. Does the Prime Minister say that is the basis of his policy?

In so far as there is any indication in its report of the course to be pursued, that course is directly contrary to the one the government has taken. Here is what the committee recommended. What action?
It is suggested that the Canadian representatives in attendance at the next meeting of the International Institute of Agriculture should be given authority to see that the matter is thoroughly discussed, in order to discover whether an international system of control is feasible through such agency.
I wonder if there is any family resemblance between that suggestion, which at least shows that the committee had some enlightened understanding of the problem, and that which is embodied in this resolution? Then the report goes on:

speechtext:
If they are in line with
those I have read I do not see what the purpose of the interruption was. That is what the committee recommended. Even the committee did not feel that to discuss the problem intelligently and to get to anything in the way of an expeditious and wise conclusion the facts were still well enough under command; and they recommended this:
In view of the important and widespread information collected during the sittings of your committee and the impossibility of digesting and properly weighing the evidence in the time at their disposal before prorogation, your committee respectfully recommend that a similar committee be appointed at an early period of the next session of parliament.
This recommendation, I would presume, has reference to other subjects under review by the committee, just as it has to this one. These three recommendations which the committee made the government has flouted, and they come to this House and say they base their policy upon the committee's report! This idea is a lately generated one of basing the government's policy upon the committee's report.
Mr. Preston has been referred to in this debate. The government seemed very sensitive as to the reputation of Mr. Preston, but no member of this side of the House has ever so reflected on that gentleman as has the Prime Minister himself. In March of 1924 Mr. Preston is sent over to investigate and report on this problem. That is the commission given him by the order in council. It is all the order in council says, except to specify his pay, which I venture to think was the most important part of the whole enterprise. After sending Mr. Preston over in March, 1924, to investigate and report, this government came to a policy without waiting for his report at all. The Prime Minister stands now and says that it does not matter at all what is in Mr. Preston's report; that he is not basing his policy on Preston's report in any way at all; he is basing his policy on the report of the Mc-Master committee, which recommended movement and action in directly the opposite way.
Now what is this government policy? It is embodied in a contract which we are asked to ratify. I am going to analyze this contract, not in any technical spirit; I am going to try and reveal to the House just what the effect of the contract is. I know the Prime Minister says: Well, it does not matter what is there; the government is going to do so and so, anyway. Mr. Speaker, there are a class of people in everyday life who, when they make a contract, do what they like irrespective of it, but I do not think parliament should accept with placidity the declaration of a Prime Minister that he is going to follow in those footsteps.
In the first place, though I do not consider this of major importance, the covenant of Sir William Petersen, that the terms, such as they are, on his part of this contract, will be carried out, is a covenant which Sir William Petersen can set fire to just as soon as the contract is implemented by this parliament.
Ocean Shipping Rates

By the way, one would think this government was entitled to some superior benediction, because, forsooth, it did not make a contract except "subject to the ratification of parliament." "We made it in this case," the Prime Minister says, "very clear to Sir William Petersen that the contract could not take effect till parliament ratified it. That is the course we pursued." Well, there was no other course on earth he could pursue. The government had absolutely no power to make a contract save subject to the will of parliament. No contract ever was made-not previously authorized by parliament-except subject to the ratification of parliament. When Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1898 brought down the Yukon railway contract, he brought it down subject to the ratification of parliament. When in 1903 he brought down the Grand Trunk Pacific contract, it was signed and sealed, and he brought it down subject to the ratification of parliament. When in 1918 the government of the day brought down the bill for taking over the Grand Trunk railway, embodying a contract, it also was subject to the ratification of parliament. All must be; the Prime Minister had no option; there was nothing else he could do. But there is this difference: In every one of those cases the government of the day, under Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and under Sir Robert Borden, took the full responsibility for their contract. They declared to parliament: This contract embodies terms which in our judgment are fair; those terms were signed and sealed; parliament can reject the contract if it will, but if it rejects that contract it rejects the government. Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Sir Robert Borden, and the present Prime Minister each of them said: "The contract is here for approval or disapproval; it cannot be trimmed." But Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Sir Robert Borden each stood by his assertion, stood by it in the face of opposition, stood up manfully and accepted his responsibility, and staked his government on the issue. But the Prime Minister in this administration wriggled and wiggled around and tried to read what he calls a principle into the resolution. He says to hon. gentlemen: If you do not like the resolution, amend it. If you do not like the contract, amend it, and we will go to Sir William Petersen and fall at his feet and ask him to accept your will. But if you won't have anything to do with it at all, throw it out, and give us something else. In a word, go on, do anything you likj, but save our precious lives.
Now I come to the contract. Sir William Petersen, immediately he forms his com-

pany, has the government bound to accept that company. Whether it is a mere watered stock company, whether it is a mere cipher without financial responsibility, it does not matter. The government has no security at all, and no lawyer of Mr. Lafleur's standing ever in his life signed his name to a statement that Sir William Petersen has not power to release himself from every covenant by the formation of a company and the substitution of that company for himself.
I do not need to read all the introductory paragraphs. I fancy they are the intellectual harvest of the government, rather than of Mr. Lafleur. I have seen documents that eminent counsel have drawn, but I never saw any other of them preceded by a lot of political fanfare such as constitutes the best portion of this contract.
The covenants on the part of Sir William Petersen are as follows. He covenants, first of all, that he shall, either by himself or by this company:
Build, equip, provide, establish and during this contract, continue and in the manner hereinafter mentioned, operate a regular shipping service between such ports in Great Britain or Ireland or the continent of Europe, and Canadian ports as may be designated by the Minister o.f Trade and Commerce for Canada or his representatives from time to time.
Will hon. members see the limitations of that covenant? He must build, equip, provide, establish and during the contract continue in the manner hereinafter mentioned to operate a regular shipping service between ports in Canada and Great Britain or the continent to be designated by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. That covenant, of course, he must keep.
Then by (b) he must:
Establish and continue and maintain and operate as hereinafter set out the shipping service hereinbefore referred to free from the control of and independent of the Atlantic shipping combine or conference or any other combine or conference now in existence or which may.be operated or established upon the Atlantic ocean at any time in the future without the sanction of the government of Canada.
First, he must build, equip and operate a regular shipping service, and the government can fix the ports; second, he must keep out of
the Atlantic Steamship conference. Those are the two covenants.
The next is-it is not in very good English, but that does not matter very much:
(c) That such service shall be put in effect and maintained with ten ships as hereinbefore referred to and these shall be built and placed in operation with all possible despatch and shaill be fully completed and put in service within eighteen months from the date of this agreement (at least two of the same to be placed in service by August 1, 1925) and pending completion of the same, other ships of modern construction properly equipped and of approximately the same tonnage-

Ocean Shipping Rates
Mark that.
-shall be substituted and operated in the said service until the fleet in question is completely constructed and in operation, the said service to commence with at least six ships not later than June 15. 1925.
That is to say, Sir William Petersen in the execution of his covenant shall have in operation by June 15, six ships of about the same tonnage as those described at the close of the agreement, and he shall have two of the new ones not later than August 1, 1925. It will be observed that the ships which he may substitute do not need to be of the speed or of any of the characteristics of those provided for in the contract; they need only to be of about the same tonnage. The next covenant is this:
(d) That the control and regulation of the rates to be charged by the contractor shall rest with the government of Canada and that the government shall fix such transportation rates on all commodities from time to time.
Let me consider this paragraph for a moment -and I do so with the open invitation to any member of the House who disagrees with me to say so. Let me discuss what is the alpha and omega, the beginning and the end, of that covenant. It gives the government of Canada the right to fix the rates on any and all commodities. Of that there is no question. But what is its meaning? The government, in respect of any commodity-and "commodity" has a distinct meaning-can say to Sir William Petersen that the rate shall be so much on his vessels. This the government can do, and no more. Under that covenant the government cannot compel Sir William Petersen to carry the commodity at the rate fixed. He may fill his ship with other commodities whose rates are fixed to his liking. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald, Pictou) takes refuge in a smile. I invite him to dispute that position.

If any hon. gentleman can suggest that any further covenant that Sir William Petersen enters into modifies in any degree the proposition I have advanced, I would feel indebted to him if he would make his suggestion now. Apparently they did not
know him. WThat was the Prime Minister's answer? The answer was this: that he supposed it was on account of the differential against Canada that the rates were so high; they were stifling business and the boats could not get traffic. So the reason the merchant marine does not make money at the high rates of the combine is because it is charging higher rates into our ports-because the rates to Canadian ports, he says, are higher than to the American. This is the reason he says the merchant marine does not pay- and the merchant marine is owned by the government which complains against the extortion. This government stands here and confesses that for three years it has kept a merchant marine under a directorate which is holding rates so high that the trade of Canada is being strangled, that our manufacturers are being stifled, that our western cattle trade is being smothered. The same merchant marine is also, he says, killing itself because its rates are so high it cannot get the business. Is that not a magnificent way to manage the merchant marine of this country? That is precisely what the Prime Minister has proclaimed.
-(An hon. Member. See p. 1248.)
Ocean Shipping Rates

Then, the Prime Minister made special reference to the cattle business. One would think from one portion of his address that the ships were to carry cattle all the time, but if they devoted all their time to carrying cattle they could not possibly carry more than half the cattle shipped. You cannot pile all the cattle over into the British market all at once. This subsidy, distributed over the cattle business, would mean a cost of about $60 a head-that is, over all this one line could carry. What an economical way to develop the Canadian cattle trade! Then, we are told that our own ships are not fit for *;he carrying of cattle. Our twenty-six ships can be fitted for cattle just 'the same as any other ships. As a matter of fact the directorate have already fitted out not less than five; at least four are running, fitted for the cattle trade, and they are carrying cattle at $20 a head. The government say, "Oh, this is doing harm to Canada, we cannot stand such a rate." The government goes to Sir William Petersen, and I just picture to myself the spectacle which was presented. Am I putting the matter one whit different from its true perspective? The Prime Minister, or say the Minister of Trade and Commerce, goes to Sir William Petersen and says: "There are our ships, we are charging $20 a head on cattle. Vv c and our fellow pirates are strangling the western cattle trade. We are throttling the Ontario cattle trade. A member of parliament gets up and says we are blood-suckers. The Lethbridge Board of Trade is up in arms. We will give you, Sir William Petersen, $13,000,000 if you will come into business and force us to reduce the rate on cattle." Will even the member for Brome suggest that that is not precisely the bargain which the Minister of Trade and Commerce now submits to this parliament for ratification? I have a certificate in my hand to show that these boats can be fitted up to carry cattle, of equal capacity with the Petersen boats which are to be built.
Has anyone answered this question in the debate:	Who is to be the arbiter to decide
which of the cattle shippers, which of the grain shippers, which of the clothes-pin shippers, which of the dairy shippers-which of all these are going to get special favours at the expense of the people of Canada? This argument would apply to merchant marine management on a low rate basis just the same as to Petersen's ships-this is precisely why we did not run the merchant marine on a scale differing from the other scales in and out of Atlantic ports. We would then have had to select special shippe.s in Canada and give them special favours at the expense of the country.

We would only have been contributing out of the treasury of Canada for the benefit of special individuals. But that is just what this government proposes to do, and besides for every dollar it gives the favoured individual, it gives Sir William Petersen two; that is the only difference. Who is to stand on the dock in Montreal and say to the shipper from one elevator. "We will give you the special low rate on wheat to-day, and say to the shipper from another: You will have to hire one of these other boats that are in the combine." Has this country any right to distinguish as between shippers? This country cannot possibly operate the government's plan without doing so; there is no way in which it can be done. Either this government or Sir William Petersen himself will be the bestower of the favours. Is the government prepared to hand over .to a man not even a citizen of Canada the right to select pets in this Dominion, and give to these pets special rates across the Atlantic? This whole thing is built on a fallacy; it is unsound from the first word to the last, and I cannot help but think that the government's only hope is to find for it a secluded cemetery at the hands of this committee. Parliament is continually being told: If you like this thing, applaud it, but if you do not like it, refer it to a committee. Such is the government's move every time when its proposals, ill-digested, come before parliament for adoption.
Hon. members, those of us who have been in the House some time, can remember that it is not many years since the chief article of faith of hon. gentlemen opposite was that the money of this country had to be spent in Canada, that no money voted by this parliament should go to help build up the shipbuilding or other industry in another land. When the government of the day in 1912-1913 proposed the construction of three ships of war of the highest scientific type ever known, by way of assistance to Great Britain under the shadow of the German menace, hon. gentlemen opposite fought it for days and weeks and months, and the chief article of opposition was that our $30,000,000 was going to be spent in shipyards overseas, and not to help -build up the shipbuilding industry in this Dominion. The government of the day felt that as we had never built anything of this type before, and as in our belief the menace was near, the only effective way was to get them built as fast as we could. We could not have established the necessary docks and all the other facilities in time. But hon. gentlemen opposite were willing to risk everything just to get those ships built in Canada. When

Ocean Shipping Rates
later in 1918 we came to the programme of constructing merchant ships in this Dominion, we took care that every one of them was built in Canadian yards, because the ships were of far simpler construction.
These ships Sir William Petersen is going to build are ships the like of which have been built in this Dominion before. They are vessels which can be built nearly as expeditiously in this country as in any other, perhaps not quite so cheaply, but better pay something more to give work to the unemployed in this country than send our money somewhere else in order to give work to the unemployed over there. The Prime Minister says: Oh, this money is not going to build ships at all; Sir William Petersen is going to provide the money to build these ships. Yes, in a way that is true, but Sir William Petersen provides the money on the faith of these subsidies. These subsidies out of the treasury of Canada are the security on which he gets his money. The money of this country in effect is to be spent in the shipyards of the old land or of Germany or somewhere over there, and according to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) the contracts are already let. The money of this country is to be spent at a time when we have tens and hundreds of thousands of unemployed, to build ships in other lands. For this purpose the government will bestow on Sir William Petersen and a company which undoubtedly will register the ships overseas, $13,000,000 out of the overstocked treasury of the Dominion of Canada.
On every count there has been failure to review, failure to consider the circumstances, failure to delve to the heart of the difficulty. There has been nothing but a hasty, ill-considered, reckless plunge; and the government hope, I suppose, because of its mere recklessness, because of the spectacular character of this legislation; that in some way they are going to attract attention to the question, and finally drift to a solution. The Prime Minister says you cannot get any arrangement for supervision as called for in the amendment. Then before he is through with his speech he says: Just let us take this plunge into the Petersen contract; just let us get beside Mr. Preston with his pebble and help him throw it into the Atlantic. In that way we will rouse the dry bones of New Zealand. We will waken Australia, and bring England to her senses, and they will all come and gather round us, and we will be able to find some sort of board or institute, which will control rates on the water. Does the Prime Minister really believe that? Do you get any further in the solution of a question by starting with a false step? If hon. members feel they do, then they ought to vote for this contract.
I go back to 1903. Did we advance the solution of the railway problem in Canada by hastily plunging into the madness of the Transcontinental? Did we? Did not we rather deter the solution? Did not we rather intensify the difficulty of the problem for a period of at least half a century?
Did we in 1922 hasten the solution of the wheat marketing problem in the west by the gold-brick legislation of that year? Did not we as a matter of fact-and I appeal to hon. gentlemen to my left-did not we really defer the solution of that problem, which now is under way, for one year, if not two? That was precisely the effect.
Did we in 1923 advance the solution of the question of high freight rates on the Great Lakes by the legislation of the Minister of Trade and Commerce of that day? Will hon. gentlemen suggest for one minute that we did? We brought in some legislation-and in that too Mr. Preston was the moving spirit from the beginning, the same man who has wound his maladorous trail through our politics for a quarter of a century-we plunged into a piece of legislation which resulted only in this, a cost of at least $3,800,000 to our western farmers in freight rates over what the American farmer was paying who enjoyed American boats. Such was the result, at the expense of the Canadian farmer. But it was not the only result. Another result was that we forced this country to the position of bending its knee to the American boat owner, and begging him to come back into our trade and violate our law. We got nothing in the wake of that hasty legislation, save a loss of millions to our farmers and a bitter humiliation to our country.
But the government says: Take this step; plunge right in, and if you cannot say anything else for us, please say that we are courageous. The Minister of Railways admits himself they are courageous. Well if courage consists in ill-considered and precipitated legislation, then the government undoubtedly is deserving of that meed of praise. Or if courage consists in prodigality with other people's money, then the members of this administration will leave a memory which will outlive the name of Joan of Arc. Courage, forsooth, to dip into the treasury of this country in a mad expenditure of $13,000,000 to do something we can do without a dollar of this expenditure at all! This contract is to be blessed by parliament, and we are expected to vote for its ratification because, if the government in proposing it have
Ocean Shipping Rates

no other virtue, they have the virtue of courage I
No; you do not advance the solution of the problem by first taking a step in the wrong direction. You thwart the solution, you delay it; and what is more you make your country a by-word before the world. What position is this country in as respects the Great Lakes problem to-day? Are we as far ahead as we were in 1923? We have a board which is forced to sham because it is supposed to be controlling rates, but everyone knows that it has not dictated a single rate. That board in actual practice, has no more to do with the control of rates on our lakes than have the wardens of a Confucian temple in Shanghai. The government may have expected that by taking that step in 1923 they would bring the American government to attention, and that the American government would join them in some system of control. But instead the American government stood by and laughed, and after the whole farce is over, the North American continent laughs as well.
Surely this House, merely because it is told by the Prime Minister that it is a case of being either in favour of low freight rates or against them, is not going to vote for this resolution. Surely this House is not going to pass its blessing on a resolution or on the ratification of a contract in which, I venture to say, in his heart of hearts no hon. member believes. I ask, subject to correction:	Is
there any hon. member who has heard this contract approved by any respectable citizen in this country outside the walls of this House? If any one can mention a man who has approved it to his face let him say who that man is. I stand and say definitely that not one human being has ever in my hearing or by letter expressed in the slightest degree any word of favor for this contract. The House is asked in the face of the direct challenge of the amendment to declare that this agreement ought to be ratified, and its feelings are soothed by the Prime Minister who says that all we really declare, is that we should like to see something done. I appeal to this House, on the contrary to make its real will known and to say that even though the government resolution be amended in detail, it is fundamentally wrong in principle, is ill-advised, costly and futile, and deserves no further consideration at the hands of parliament.

My . hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) has read isolated quotations from his remarks, but I am in the judgment of the House if the trend of his remarks all through was not along the line that there was no necessity for dealing with this matter in the way the government were proposing to do, because there was not a combine in the sense in which it was charged. I would not wilfully misrepresent my hon. friend in any way. but I am quite sure that the impression which was left upon my mind and the mind of every hon. gentleman by the tone of his remarks was such as I have indicated. I am sure my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen), when he announced this afternoon that there was no question about there being a combine, and then began to coo and to indulge in that kind of remarks, which he can do so easily, intimating that after all there might be worse things than combines, particularly in regard to shippers, took a very peculiar position. There were other days when he did not coo so sweetly in regard to combines, but thundered at them in the most vehement way. Hon. gentlemen who were in the House in 1913 will remember that my right hon. friend at that time thought the situation in regard to the Atlantic freight rates had reached so serious a position that he moved the adjournment of the House in order to call attention of the House and the country to its importance and made a demand that the then government which he was supporting take some immediate action to deal with it. And well might he do so, because here in Canada, with our immense undeveloped resources, unless we find an outlet for our
Ocean Shipping Rates

export trade under conditions under which we can profitably send what we produce to the older nations of the world, we have but very little hope for or confidence in our future. In exporting the products of the farm, the mines and other industries, we are in competition with the United States of America, with the Argentine Republic and with the other overseas dominions all of whom are as yet in a somewhat similar position to that in which we find ourselves. Yet my hon. friend, in 1913, realizing the seriousness of the situation moved, as is customary in cases of urgency, that the House should adjourn in order to enable him to bring the situation before parliament and the country. What did he say at that time? He said:
I have placed before you, Mr. Speaker, a somewhat elaborate table showing the great increase that has taken place in ocean rates on grain and flour. That increase cannot be accounted for by normal conditions of any kind and in my judgment an explanation can be found only in a condition of affairs such as we have been compelled to address ourselves to in other lines of industry, namely the presence of monopoly. What is the monopoly that appears to be in control in this instance? There is no attempt to keep secret the fact that there exists an understanding between the various steamship lines operating between north America and European and particularly United Kingdom ports. It is known as the Canadian North Atlantic west bound freight conference. That conference, however, took its birth not at the time that the rates were increased in this way. That conference has been an institution of very oonsiiderable strength for the last eight years. It has been doing its work in a thorough method. For the first three or four or five years of its existence apparently it devoted its energy to sweeping from ,the high seas traversed by its lines all of what are known as tramp steamers, those steamships that have operated through many years as the element that introduced real competition in freight rates over the Atlantic.
Again he says:
As I showed at the commencement, this conference has so successfully done its work that roughly speaking they have raised incoming freight rates from twenty to fifty per cent, and in some cases by even a larger percentage, in that way largely nullifying any advantage we might hope to secure from the British preference.
And yet he produced tables this afternoon from the London Economist in which the rates from this side of the Atlantic, both from the United States and Canada, were shown with a view of answering these large specific increases in rates which my right hon. friend and leader (Mr. Mackenzie King) gave to the House on Tuesday night. My right hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) attempted to make it appear to the House and the country that the actual increase in freight rates in Canada. was not as great as it really is, and yet he inveighed against them at that time and said:

Furthermore it is wall known, and, I think, uncontradicted that those lines which operate from our ports to ports across the Atlantic have a distinct understanding, if not more than that, with all lines operating from Portland and the port of New York to similar ports across the ocean. All have been brought under what is known as the North Atlantic Shipping conference. They are all reaping the rewards that come from that monopolistic corporation and they all at present feel themselves bound to obey the dictates of that conference, whatever they may be. The problem that faces us is this. Is it possible, and along what lines is it possible, to succeed so as to bring to a sense of duty, to a sense of equity, this corporation? I do not think I am stating the case too strongly when I say that there is a monopoly. We have every evidence of a monopoly in the arrogant exercise of power that we have had to submit to up to the present time. I am aware that the government have been dealing with this matter; that they have addressed themselves to it with vigour. I am also well aware that it is not possible to follow the old methods of attack and hope to meet with success in an attack on this corporation. It is not possible to adopt the old weapons and hope to win. Along what lines is it possible that we may succeed ?

speechtext:
When my
right hon. friend, who is such a severe critic, had the responsibility as Prime Minister of this country, after initiating a discussion of this subject in 1913, I am in the judgment of this House whether, from what has taken place here at this moment, the right hon. gentleman ever took one step in order to deal with the matter. He writes to Dr. Magill, he never inquires to find out whether Dr. Magill has made an investigation or not, and he leaves the matter there. That is where my right hon. friend stands in regard to this question. In dealing with the subject under discussion this afternoon, my right hon. friend asserts that we cannot control cur rates on Canadian exports. This is quite at variance with his attitude previously when he demanded that the government of the day should take some action in regard to it; but he was unable to advise, because my right hon. friend is usually destructive, and I am in the judgment of the House and the country if my right hon. friend ever signalized his responsibility by any constructive method or movement dn regard to any matter. To-day he says that the rates cannot be controlled. In the case of a combine, I should like to know as a business proposition if there is any way in which you can prevent that combine from operating except by creating competition for it. That is a sound and sensible proposition. If you have a certain group of people that control a condition of affairs in any kind of business, must you not find competition in order to remedy the matter in some way? If you cannot find the existing competition, must you not create that competition, which, by its entry into the field, will enable the article to be manufactured at a cheaper price or to be carried at a lower rate than that which the combine imposes?
My right hon. friend indicated that we had done nothing after the report of the McMaster committee, as it is known. My right hon. friend entirely omitted, when the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) asked him to read further this afternoon, a certain recommendation that was made at that time. That recommendation reads:
Should it appear that there are no ships or not a sufficient number of ships belonging to the Canadian
Ocean Shipping Bates

Government Merchant Marine suitable for this service then it would appear that wisdom would dictate the disposal of some of the smaller ships to enable ships of the class required to be secured.
He failed this afternoon to mention that. He read a recommendation to take the matter up at the Economic conference. The Minister of Railways and Canals and the then Minister of Justice brought before the conference committee and the Imperial Shipping committee the rates on flour and other rates which were urged upon them at that time, and as a result of their efforts a sub-committee of the shipping committee came to Canada last year and dealt with that question by way of investigation. A matter of this kind cannot be dealt with in a moment. The government have been active in considering how this great problem, so vital to the business interests of this country, might be grappled with in some way and how these results might be obtained. We have now submitted to the judgment of parliament the proposal which we have before us. My right hon. friend was very much worried because this proposal was going to a special committee. Is there any reason why it should not? Time and again, in a somewhat lengthy parliamentary experience, I have known governments to submit measures to the House and to say that, instead of the ordinary procedure which applies to government bills of going into committee of the Whole, after second readings, they propose to submit them to the consideration of a special committee in order that the whole House may be thoroughly seized of the matter. How much more on a great question of this kind would the government be justified in taking this course of submitting this measure to a special committee, so that it might be closely and completely scrutinized and we might arrive at some solution of the problem in the best interests of the people of this country? Now my right hon. friend engaged in some casuistical criticisms of this contract. In the first place, he told us that Sir William Petersen need only have one sailing a year. Well, Mr. Speaker, there is not much use discussing before the House in great detail what the legal effect of a contract may be, but this is the plain English of the contract in regard to this matter, that the contractor shall-
Build, equip, provide, establish and during this contract, continue and in the manner hereinafter mentioned, operate a regular shipping service between such ports in Great Britain or Ireland or the continent of Europe, and Canadian ports as may be designated by the Minister of Trade and Commerce for Canada or his representatives from time to time.
I had the opportunity of conferring with the distinguished legal gentleman who passed

upon this contract, I refer to Mr. Lafleur, and it is his judgment, with all due deference to my right hon. friend's experience, and it is my judgment, if it is worth anything, that that clause has only one meaning-that a regular shipping service is a continuous shipping service throughout the year. Not only that, but my right hon. friend went on to say that it was not Canadian goods that were to be carried; all kinds of goods could be carried without the government here having anything to say about it. Well, it is the a, b. c of legal construction that when you are dealing with the interpretation of a contract you look to the recitals in order to see the purpose and object expected to be secured by the operative clauses later on. And this is one of the recitals:
And whereas the government, of Canada after an investigation of the representations brought to its knowledge and after giving the same serious consideration has thought it wise to adopt such means as may he deemed expedient and necessary to exercise such supervision and control of trans-Atlantic freight rates as it is .possible for them to do and thereby as far as possible to prevent and defeat any unreasonable excess or overcharge in ocean freight rates as exercised by such ocean shipping combines or conferences to the loss and detriment of its citizens and has reached the conclusion that in order to more fully safeguard the interests of its citizens it would be well advised to enter into an arrangement whereby it may exercise such control or supervision and whereby it may improve the conditions under which the products of its citizens are exported or imported.
That recital contains the express purpose of the contract, it is a controlling clause, and not even a barrister of a year's experience would venture to assert before any court in this country that it had any other meaning, nor, I venture to say, would any judge for one moment listen to an argument that the government of Canada had no control over the commodities that were to be carried by these ships. The language in regard to the control of rates is also so clear and definite that it cannot be considered for one moment as capable of any other construction:
That the control and regulation of the rates to be charged by the contractor shall rest with the government of Canada and that the government shall fix such transportation rates on all commodities from time to time.

speechtext:
I was dealing with the question of rates and the question whether it was Canadian goods that were to be carried on these ships. I will come to my hon. friend's point in due course, but he is not going to be permitted to divert the attention of the House from the point which I am making at this time-that absolutely and beyond a shadow of a doubt under this contract the control of rates and the control of goods that are to be exported vests in the government of Canada.
Then my right hon. friend indulged in some pyrotechnics in regard to the law concerning lake freight rates. Let us be frank and understand where we are with respect to that question. A commission was appointed, composed of Mr. McLean, of the railway commission, Mr. Thompson of Saskatchewan and General Tremblay, who is connected with shipping in Quebec. That commission recommended to the attention of the House and the government the measure which we submitted in accordance with the terms of that recommendation. That is where the law came from. It was created after the fullest investigation by a commission whose members certainly were in a position to examine the subject thoroughly.
Now I propose to deal with the question generally, and to call the attention of the House to what the government has done in regard to this contract. We have chartered ten new vessels, fully equipped for our trade, and we have obtained control of the movements of these vessels, and of the rates to be charged. The contract is substantially a charter party, similar to what might be entered into by any business firm engaged in a large way in the transportation of its products. We make the charter party and place the ships at the disposal of the Canadian producer and manufacturer, with the certainty that they will be able to transport their products cheaper than they can now, and with the assurance that those products will be transported through Canadian ports. That is a summary of our policy. That is the result we obtain by the arrangement we have made, and no amount of argument can gainsay it. This talk of handing 813,000,000 out of the treasury for no return entirely overlooks the substantial results that are involved in this contract. If we had a large business firm in Canada producing some staple product of which it was able to make large sales in Great Britain or on the continent, what would it do? It would proceed to make an arrangement with a shipping firm owning and controlling a fleet of ships to carry its products. In a word, it would make a charter
party under which it would pay the shipping firm so much for the service to be rendered. That is what we have done. We pay this money in order that we may control these rates in the interests of the Canadian people, in order that these ships will sail from Canadian ports, and in order that the present condition of affairs under which our ports are discriminated against in favour of United States ports will not be permitted to continue. That is what we have done. And why should not that measure be submitted to a committee of this House?
In a speech in 1913 my right hon. friend indicated that the British interests in this matter were adverse to ours. They certainly are. Let us be frank about this. Sir George Perley says so. Writing to my right hon friend in 1920 Sir George said:
The terms of reference do not definitely give the committee-
That is, the Imperial Shipping committee
authority to consider the possibility of controlling freight rates, but I explained fully to the committee at their first meeting the interest which Canada took in that question.
Then again he wrote:
As such a large amount of tonnage is owned in these Islands they are perhaps naturally not very anxious about the control of freight rates and therefore, if you decide to bring the question before the committee, I do not think it possible to give too much time or attention to the preparation of our case.
Then my right hon. friend asked Dr. Magill to prepare a case, but never once inquired whether he had done so or not. Now, what is the situation in regard to our relation to the Mother Country in reference to shipping? My hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean) in the resolution which he introduced some weeks ago in favour of Canada having the power to amend her constitution, asserted, and asserted vociferously, that all we needed to do was to ask the Mother Country and she would grant us our request. My hon. friend entirely forgot the relation in which we stand to the Mother Country with regard to shipping. Section 91 of the British North America Act purports to give Canada the right to deal with navigation and shipping. But let me tell the House, we cannot deal with navigation and shipping except in a bettered way. Under the Merchant Shipping Act of 1854, which was re-enacted in 1894, Canada cannot do a single thing in regard to shipping except as to shipping which is registered in this country. Let us see how that works out-and it explains some of the difficulties we have to contend with in dealing with this matter. It is quite time that this House and the country
Ocean Shipping Rates

realized the larger issue that is involved in this question. The Hon. Mr. Brodeur, late Judge of the Supreme Court of Canada, whose unfortunate demise occurred a short time ago, when he was Minister of Marine and Fisheries previous to 1911 took up with the British authorities the question of amendments to the existing law which would enable us to deal freely with these matters as we can deal with other matters committed to us. Australia and New Zealand, in state papers, presented to the British government a similar claim and are still pressing the matter. Under the Merchant Shipping Act, so called, British shipping, Australian shipping, New Zealand shipping, can engage in our coasting trade and we cannot do anything to prevent it, to interfere with it, even to regulate it. If, for instance, Canada desired to impose a duty upon ships built in Great Britain and brought over here, that duty would be entirely nugatory, because if the ships were registered in Great Britain they would have a right to engage in our coasting trade and we could not interfere with them in any way. Not only that: we passed in 1910 the Canadian Carriage of Goods Act under which we undertook to lay down the rules applicable to bills of lading upon export cargoes from Canada. The Furness-Withy people and others engaged in this absolutely ignore that act; they make their bills of lading as they please, because, they say, if the ships are registered in Great Britain they are not amenable to our laws; the Canadian Carriage of Goods Act does not apply. Under the Colonial Laws Validity Act we cannot legislate in regard to any question affecting for instance, the amount of money recoverable in the case of a collision at sea; nor can we make any amendments to the rules of practice of the Admiralty court unless we secure approval through an imperial order in council. My right hon. friend was quite right in 1913, and Sir George Perley was quite right in 1920, when they said that the British people were not in favour of the control of rates or of giving us anything to say in regard to that matter. The shipping interest in England is very powerful, controlling as it does, political situations, dictating legislation and generally occupying probably the strongest position of any business interest in the great Mother Country. And they do not want their rates controlled; they would not agree to any proposal looking to the control of rates in Great Britain. We might as well bay at the moon as expect them to do anything in that connection. Though my right hon. friend had two resolutions drawn on this question,-and his supporter from 
Burrard (Mr. Clark) moved one here-he knew very well that the effect of that resolution if adopted would be to negative any chance of our getting an improvement in the matter of freight rates.

I will make this statement, and my right hon. friend will not dispute it: The British parliament will not agree to legislation that will provide for the control of rates on British shipping. This is the way this Shipping committee, according to their own story, had the matter of flour dealt with-I quote from their report:
We are pleased to say that we were able to obtain a satisfactory undertaking from the Canadian Liner committee-
That is the graceful title which means North Atlantic combine.
-in regard to discrimination in rates against Canadian flour. This no doubt should be supported by a fur ver

Ocean Shipping Rates
undertaking on the part of the British lines engaged in the north Atlantic trade, if such an undertaking can be obtained.
It has also been suggested that this board got something done in regard to insurance on the matter being brought before them. What was done was this-a very anomalous thing: the insurance rates which have discriminated so completely against our Canadian ports and in favour of New York and Portland, as indicated by my right hon. friend and leader when he read from the report of Mr. Scott, the grain commissioner, the other day, has been changed so that the rate is somewhat lower on the hulls of vessels sailing from Halifax, but the insurance rate has not been decreased one cent upon the cargoes going in those same vessels. A very peculiar anomaly, is it not? Nor has the port of St. John, which is our larger Maritime seaport, been able to get its insurance rates reduced at all, either on hulls or on cargoes. So that the remedy suggested in the resolution moved by the hon. member for Burrard simply puts this proposal into a political cemetery whence it can never be resurrected in our time. It relegates to oblivion the idea that any relief whatever can be obtained for this country in the matter of ocean freight rates.
My right hon. friend spoke this afternoon on the question of the utilization of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, and I want to discuss very frankly that phase of the subject. I have gone into that matter and I find that of the ships of the Canadian merchant marine, 23 are under 5,000 tons. Fourteen are on the Great Lakes or laid up and are therefore not available for ocean tonnage. Thirteen are used in the Pacific trade and have, I understand, been successful in developing trade on the Pacific coast, sailing from Vancouver to other ports. Fifteen are engaged an the Australian trade taking in New Zealand and other places. Six are in the West Indian trade and nine on the north Atlantic. Those in the West Indian trade are being sailed there in accordance with the treaty arrangements which were made with the West Indies.
