direct the attention of the House to a clause in the contract to which my right hon. friend did not refer:
And it is mutually covenanted and agreed between the parties hereto that the shipping services to be established by the contractor herein will co-operate and work loyally with the Canadian National Railways system and the fleet of ships operated by that system and under its control and known as the Canadian Government Merchant Marine.
The purpose of the government in regard to this matter is to ask the Canadian Government Railways, which are operating these ships, to work in conjunction with the ships that are to be constructed under this contract, so that co-operating together, and with the facilities of the railway being available for both the Petersen ships as well as our own, we shall have in reality 19 ships with which to deal with this combine.
You may ask, why was it not done before? Here was the situation. >Here was this immense deficit upon the railways, and a deficit on the merchant marine ships. Now the proposition that you are going to fight a combine with nine ships, without any reserves of strength of any kind, I am sure every hon. gentleman will agree with me, on reflection, was not a sound business one, if the matter was being handled directly by the government. We had before us the result of the experience of the United States and of Australia, both of whom have gone out of operating their ships directly. The solution of the problem rests now on the arrangement we have made
Ocean Shipping Rates

with Sir William Petersen for ten ships under charter, together with the nine ships, if not more, of the government merchant marine on the north Atlantic co-operating with the Canadian National railways, with their freight rates controlled, and their destinations controlled. In that way we shall have given to Canada, when this contract is approved by parliament, the first practical method of dealing with this vexed question in this country.

the intention of the government to place the merchant marine vessels under the management of Sir William Petersen?

speechtext:
I should
think the government would see its way clear
to supplement in connection with the government merchant marine vessels, just the same as they would in regard to the Petersen boats, although we are obtaining control of the rates on the Petersen boats as the result of a special charter.
Let us never forget what the situation is in regard to the Petersen contract. We hear a lot of talk about subsidies, but I assert this, and I venture to say it cannot be gainsaid: that what we have done in regard to the Petersen contract is simply to charter these ten vessels when constructed, and we shall have absolute control over their rates and destinations, and all such matters, in just the same way as a business firm in this country would that chartered ten vessels from the other side of the ocean. That is the sum and substance of the situation from a legal standpoint. There is no more technical and difficult subject to deal with, as a matter of law and business, than shipping and shipping contracts, and hon. gentlemen who have high status at the bar, but who have not had an opportunity of living at the seaboard,

where they would come into contact with shipping business, have-no matter what their status may be-very little knowledge of how these problems are worked out. So technical is this shipping business and shipping law that not only in the Mother Country but in the seaboard provinces of this Dominion, both on the Atlantic and on the Pacific, men have given up practically all their other legal business in order to devote themselves to shipping law and shipping business. I assert, with some experience in these matters, because coming from a seaboard province I have had to deal with them, that all this talk about subsidies, all this bugaboo that is raised on the question, is simply an attempt to mislead the public mind in regard to what is a simple business proposition. This country is simply chartering from Sir William Petersen ten ships for ten years, and instead of giving him so much per ton, we are paying him a flat rate. In regard to the utilization of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine ships, it is both implied and expressly stated in the contract that the Petersen ships in working out the contract shall work in conjunction and unison with the Canadian Government Railway system, and with the fleet of ships operated by that system.

speechtext: Well, for the simple reason that we look at the experience of the United States and Australia. maintopic: EARNINGS FROM A "PETERSEN" STEAMER VOYAGE IN THE SEASON 1924 (AS PUBLISHED IN "HANSARD" PAGE 723) COMPARED WITH EARNINGS BASED UPON THE AVERAGE FREIGHT RATES FOR 1913 FROM MONTREAL TO LONDON
speechtext:
My hon.
friend is very prolific of suggestions. These vessels are being run by officials connected with the Canadian National Railway system. I do not know whether they are making any mistake in running them. Probably they are running them as cheaply as they could be run anyway. My hon. friend wants us to give these ships away or to hand them over to Sir William Petersen. I do not think the Canadian people would be in favour of giving them away. But there is no reason why as a business proposition the results contemplated under this contract cannot be obtained, and I think they will be obtained, much more efficaciously along the line the government is suggesting than in the way my hon. friend suggests.
Let me say further, we have had a great deal of criticism of this proposal. My right hon. friend the leader of the opposition talked for two and a half hours this afternoon on the subject, and offered not a single constructive suggestion as to how to deal with this problem. I would like to hear, and this government and the country would lake to hear, from hon. gentlemen who are criticizing this proposal some tangible suggestion that will be an improvement upon it. If you are going to leave this question to the British shipping interests, you will never solve this problem of the combine. There is only one way to deal with a combine, and that is to give it competition. I'f there is 85
any other way, when you have not legislative control, I would like to know what it is. While, therefore, the method suggested may not be absolutely the best solution that could be devised for meeting the problem, the government submits it to the House with the proposal that a special committee be appointed to go thoroughly into the whole matter, investigating it from every angle. And I am confident that after the committee shall have heard evidence and gone into the subject fully, the conclusion will be that the method suggested by the government is a sound one. Hon. gentlemen may indulge in criticism, but if the evil was great in 1913 I think it will be admitted that it is still greater to-day. The combine has a strangle hold on the business interests of Canada, and our progress in trade is hampered in consequence. We cannot make any advancement so long as these impositions are exacted against our products as a result of the operation of any combine. It is necessary therefore, in the interests of the people at large, that we make some attempt to grapple with the situation, and I submit in confidence that the committee of the House which will scrutinize the measure with every care will give it their support.

maintopic: EARNINGS FROM A "PETERSEN" STEAMER VOYAGE IN THE SEASON 1924 (AS PUBLISHED IN "HANSARD" PAGE 723) COMPARED WITH EARNINGS BASED UPON THE AVERAGE FREIGHT RATES FOR 1913 FROM MONTREAL TO LONDON
speechtext:
In rising to make a few remarks on the resolution and the amendment thereto it would not be amiss, I think, to express the pious hope that the subject may be discussed on its merits wthout any recourse to political controversy. I had intended to offer a word of congratulation to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) on his able speech this afternoon, but I realize now that if I did so I might be treading on dangerous ground after having heard the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald, Pictou). I do not think that hon. gentleman would relish any remarks of that kind.
The resolution, I understand, was prompted by the report we have before us, submitted by Mr. Preston, the allegations in which are to the effect that there exists a shipping combine which has practically complete control over all trade routes. They operate by outbidding competing lines, thus eliminating competition, and they divide the territory

Ocean Shipping Rates

among themselves. I do not think there is any question as to the nature of the general allegation of the report-certainly the suggestion is there-that this combine is out to work against British companies and industries.
The Prime Minister in speaking the other night on this subject offered the suggestion that this report was not the only thing which the government had to inspire them to move in the direction now proposed. He told us that there was a vast amount of correspondence from certain sources pointing to the impossibility of carrying on trade under existing rates; these companies situated throughout Canada, it was stated, found it very difficult to do business, and possibly this was another source of inspiration leading to the present step on the part of the government. Be that as it may, I think we are justified in assuming that both arguments more or less influenced the government in the matter. Let me now consider the action which the government proposes to take to meet the situation. It is proposed to subsidize a certain company-I understand that the government objects to that word, but I know of no other which can exactly describe the proposal; the government, I say, intends subsidizing a company-which will enter into competition with the combine which is now in operation. Speaking the other night in this House in another connection, I recalled the condition of affairs in the late nineties in regard to the- railways in western Canada. I should like to refer to that matter again. In those days it was generally alleged that the Canadian Pacific Railway was a heartless company that operated simply for the purpose of extorting money from the poor settlers in the west, and it was urged that the only way by which that situation could be met was by building another road to com-* pete against it. We proceeded to do that, and it has been stated during this debate that the competition which is supposed to go on between the two railways is to keep them from reducing rates under governmental control. We have a railway commission which, it is said, actually precludes any possibility of the railways charging exorbitant rates. Now, so far as the export trade of western Canada is concerned, I think it is only fitting that we should consider the whole situation from the time the product is laid on the car in western points until it reaches its destination overseas. The portion of rail over which these goods are hauled is one step in the export business. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham), discussing this subject the other night, said that what the government had in
fMr. Kellner.]
mind was to establish governmental control, and I took it that he wanted that control fixed in a way similar to the control that obtains on the lakes and the railways. I think therefore that we are justified, in considering the question of ocean rates, to refer to what has been done in other departments of our export trade.
Let us take our railways. When the Crows-nest pass agreement was reinstated recently -that is to say, to the extent to which it was reinstated-the railway commission acting on behalf of the government rejected it. Of course, it was again reinstated by the Supreme court. But at the present time the Railway Act is not being enforced by any means in its entirety. There is a clause in the act providing against discrimination, and it is hard for the rank and file of western people to see why that clause is not being put into effect. Let us take now the condition on the Great Lakes; for transportation there is an important factor in our export trade. We held an investigation into that matter a couple of years ago and passed a resolution to do away with the combine that existed in that regard. It was definitely represented to the committee that investigated the subject then that there existed on the Great Lakes a combine of no uncertain potentialities. I do not know but that the evidence submitted to that committee went to show that there was as complete a combine on the Great Lakes as on the Atlantic. If I remember rightly, in the year 1922 there was an announcement that lake rates would be decreased, and the ship owners along with the Canadian railways called a meeting in Toronto to consider ways and means of maintaining the rates. Just about the time the Toronto meeting w'as called, rumour reached them that the American roads also intended reducing rates. A meeting was then called in New York at which there were representatives of the Canadian railways, the American railways and the steamship companies, and it was agreed that the American companies should not reduce their rates. So that governmental control, so far as it applies to railways and to the Great Lakes, evidently is a control which keeps them from
9	p.m. reducing rates; and if we were to establish that sort of control on the Atlantic I doubt whether we Should be able to relieve the situation which now exists.
In all fairness, it seems to me, we should inquire the personnel of the companies who comprise the combine, inasmuch as they have definitely started out for the purpose of handicapping British industry. I do not think

Ocean Shipping Rates
the statement can be challenged that they are largely British companies, consisting of men who unquestionably are high up in social and financial circles. And it seems rather a startling suggestion that they would go out and deliberately fix rates which would handicap England and would work to the benefit of other countries. I think if we delve into this great question to any depth at all we will probably find that there is something else besides the combine which is affecting these rates.
When we get down to the Great Lakes rate portion of the route, we have about a half dozen different routes which grain coming east may take. It may go down to some of the American ports and over American railroads, or may take the all-water route to Montreal, or may take the lake and rail route. We find that each year over fifty per cent goes by the American route. I do not think there is any question that the road which will carry the cheapest gets the grain. Some evidence was submitted to the committee which investigated national railways and shipping which I think shows one reason for the great percentage of our grain going out over American routes. That evidence was to the effect that grain would follow whichever route offered the best rate. If the rates are cheaper going by the American ports than by the Canadian ports, and if we give effect to this agreement and subsidize Canadian products other than grain, would that not be an incentive for the greater percentage of our grain to go by the American routes? I think, if we are going to subsidize only Canadian products going by Canadian ports, that we are actually building up a proposition which would probably divert more grain to the American routes. With reference to the ocean transport, I have before me the evidence which was submitted to the committee to which I referred as to the results of the operation of some of the merchant marine boats. The eastbound part of the first cargo paid 830,555.37. The westbound1 cargo paid S3,314.94; and the entire cargo paid $33,869.30. I would suggest that, as far as that trip is concerned, the reason that we have a high rate going to Europe is that we have no cargo coming west. If we had a cargo both ways there is no question but that the rates going east would be very much lower. This is not the only case. A long list is given here and they are pretty much on the same line. Take for instance the one that is labelled No. 16, I believe it is the Commander. The gross earnings of that boat eastbound were $38,132.74 and westbound $1,061.38. The boat S5i
was actually coming back practically empty. It would be impossible to have a low rate coming westward with a cargo amounting to a little over a thousand dollars, and apparently the only thing we can do is to increase the eastbound rates to pay for the ballast which they must carry when they are coming west. So much for the Canadian National. I have the Canadian Pacific Railway reports here-and they are sometimes spoken of as being an authority on shipping. The reports of the merchant marine show that it is all ballast coming one way. This Canadian Pacific report reads:
The Canadian Pacific steamships, in common with all other ocean lines, have in 1922 passed through a trying period. The large amount of ocean tonnage which the owners have endeavoured to keep in commission has naturally created a situation seriously affecting revenues from transportation both as to freight and passengers.
And again in 1923 they report:
The Canadian Pacific Steamships Limited, have in 1923 continued to show improvement in service and in revenues although many factors which militate against satisfactory operating results yet prevail. The world's ocean tonnage still exceeds trade requirements and financial conditions in Europe and labour unrest in Great Britain have had an adverse effect on steamship traffic.
Taking the two together their arguments would show that this trade is unbalanced and that there is too much shipping in operation, and I do not believe that a ship subsidy is going to relieve or cure that situation. I believe we will have to get something different from that. I am disposed to think that we do not give quite consideration enough to what might be done in the matter of negotiations between the government and these companies, and I am encouraged to read in that connection an item from the Commercial Intelligence Journal March 7, which says:
Mr. A. E. Bryan, Canadian trade commissioner in Kobe, has for some months past been co-operating with western cattle raisers, the federal Department of Agriculture, and the various provincial departments in an effort to open the Japanese market to shipments of Canadian cattle. In this connection the government of Alberta sent a special representative to Japan to report on the possibilities of increased shipments to that country. His investigations substantiated the opinion of the Canadian trade commissioner that any development of the trade would be impossible at the transportation rate existing, namely $75 per head from Canadian ports to Japan. After discussion, successive reductions have since been made, to $50 per head, and to $37.50, the rate now quoted by the Canadian Government Merchant Marine and the Pacific lines.
Now here is an instance where rates have been reduced, according to this article, from $75 to $37.50. I do not think the article is quite correct. I h:ive watched those negotiations with considerable interest, and I hope
Ocean Shipping Rates

the Minister of Agriculture will tell us some time what part his department took in the negotiations. I was under the impression the provincial government carried it out. I think the rate was formerly $100, reduced to $44 and eventually to $37.50. I maintain that that is just about as good or great an accomplishment as you can hope to achieve by starting up another company in competition with those that already exist. It is certainly worth trying. Mention was made the other night about the feasibility of taking over the Canadian Pacific Railway to work in conjunction with our merchant marine, and this new company which we propose to inaugurate. I should like to ask the government if, in the event of such an undertaking being arranged, would it be their opinion that they cou'ld use the anti-combine legislation to force the Canadian Pacific ships to come under a contract similar to that now proposed in reference to this subsidy. It seems to me there is a Canadian company that would be operating under Canadian registry, and it might be so that Canadian Pacific ships-

maintopic: EARNINGS FROM A "PETERSEN" STEAMER VOYAGE IN THE SEASON 1924 (AS PUBLISHED IN "HANSARD" PAGE 723) COMPARED WITH EARNINGS BASED UPON THE AVERAGE FREIGHT RATES FOR 1913 FROM MONTREAL TO LONDON
speechtext: The Canadian Pacific ships are under British, not Canadian registry. Therefore, what the hon. member suggests coulld not be accomplished.

maintopic: EARNINGS FROM A "PETERSEN" STEAMER VOYAGE IN THE SEASON 1924 (AS PUBLISHED IN "HANSARD" PAGE 723) COMPARED WITH EARNINGS BASED UPON THE AVERAGE FREIGHT RATES FOR 1913 FROM MONTREAL TO LONDON
speechtext:
I made the statement on the supposition that if the Canadian government took them over, unquestionably we could change that and they would then be operating under Canadian registry. What I was particularly anxious to find out was: Would this anti-trust law, in the opinion of the government, be elastic enough to cover this? If so, it would give us a very formidable array of ships, consisting of the present merchant marine, the Canadian Pacific and this Petersen line, if this measure is carried in t'he House. I believe, to those who sit in this corner of the House, the suggestion of taking over the Canadian Pacific makes probably the strongest appeal of all. We have for a considerable number of years been believers in government ownership, and I am disposed to think that this would meet with a hearty response from those who occupy the benches immediately surrounding me. There is one danger, I presume, in considering it at the present time, and I think the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) should have delivered his speech on the electrification of railroads at the same time. Then he would have impressed the House with the danger of getting some out-of-date equipment which we might get if we were taking the railways over at the moment. I do not, however, presume
fMr. Kellner.]
there is very great possibility of our taking them over in the near future, and we shall probably not be embarrassed by that contingency.
In reference to ocean rates, I have before me a statement of the rates charged in 1923, from May to November, and I find that unquestionably the quantity of tonnage that was offered at any port was a big factor in connection with the rates. They varied all the way from six cents to nine cents during that year. I do not think there is any question that, before we solve this problem, we shall have, by some method or another, to equalize our trade. I might throw out this suggestion to the government: There has been a good deal of agitation from this side of the House, at one time or another, to make a study of European countries which have inflated their currency. I believe, if you will look over the countries that to-day are enjoying low rates, you will find that invariably they have inflated their currency to a certain extent. My argument in that connection is that, by that inflation, they are able to start an active trade in their country. Where the trade is, the ships are going, and where the ships are going, the rates are lower. So, in all probability before we shall settle this question to the best advantage, at least, we shall have to give that some consideration. In my estimation, it would certainly be worth while having a commission appointed who would be empowered to deal with this export business and who would be given the privilege of contracting for rates. When we were considering the combine on the Great Lakes, the feature which received the most prominence about that combine was the fact that two men were able to allot the entire cargoes that went on all those boats. Supposing we give a small commission that privilege in regard to ocean freight and allow them to contract for it, it would seem to me they could get a better contract than it is possible to get when every man is doing his own business.
In conclusion, I do not think, I would fee! justified in supporting the resolution from what arguments have been submitted to the House. I think the amendment is 'probably a little drastic. The suggestion might be worthy of consideration, I do not know; I have not much faith in its accomplishing anything, but I would hardly go so far as the mover of the amendment and say that the suggestion is absolutely unworthy of our consideration.

maintopic: EARNINGS FROM A "PETERSEN" STEAMER VOYAGE IN THE SEASON 1924 (AS PUBLISHED IN "HANSARD" PAGE 723) COMPARED WITH EARNINGS BASED UPON THE AVERAGE FREIGHT RATES FOR 1913 FROM MONTREAL TO LONDON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am induced to intervene in

Ocean Shipping Rates
this debate because I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) across the floor if he approved this agreement, and his reply was to the effect that that was why the government signed it. I think the agreement is very prejudicial to the interests of the country. There are men of legal standing in the government, and it is impossible for me to conclude that that agreement was read over and considered by the lawyers in the cabinet before it was signed. My other reason for attempting to address the House is that I stated it to be my opinion that, in the final result, under this agreement the control of rates passed to Sir William Petersen and was not in the hands of the government. I hope to show this even to lay minds before I take my seat. This agreement interests me very much.
I was attracted to it by what is no part of the agreement at all. It is a peculiar thing that upon a commercial agreement there should be an affidavit of execution. This is not done in the province of Ontario where the agreement was signed.

maintopic: EARNINGS FROM A "PETERSEN" STEAMER VOYAGE IN THE SEASON 1924 (AS PUBLISHED IN "HANSARD" PAGE 723) COMPARED WITH EARNINGS BASED UPON THE AVERAGE FREIGHT RATES FOR 1913 FROM MONTREAL TO LONDON
speechtext: Nor anywhere else.

maintopic: EARNINGS FROM A "PETERSEN" STEAMER VOYAGE IN THE SEASON 1924 (AS PUBLISHED IN "HANSARD" PAGE 723) COMPARED WITH EARNINGS BASED UPON THE AVERAGE FREIGHT RATES FOR 1913 FROM MONTREAL TO LONDON
speechtext:
I thought: How did this come about? And then I noticed that the witness to the agreement and the maker of the affidavit was a judge of the Supreme court. It is suggested that Mr. Eugene Lafleur safeguarded the interests of the government in connection with this contract. I know Mr. Lafleur; I know that he is a master of the English language, and I know that this agreement was drawn by a literary sloven. It is obvious on the face of it. I also know that Mr. Lafleur is a distinguished jurisconsult, a man who understands how to draw an agreement expressing accurately the rights of the parties, and I say that this agreement was drawn by a drafting bungler. The affidavit is evidence of that. Does that affidavit serve any purpose whatever? None at all. Can any purpose ever be made of it? None at all. Sir William Petersen will never dispute the execution of the agreement and I do not think Mr. Thomas A. Low will. But supposing one or both did, you cannot prove the agreement by this affidavit. You have to call this Supreme court judge of the Yukon into the witness box and there he subjects himself to cross-examination.
I pass from this peculiar affidavit, following as it does an affidavit of execution under the Ontario statutes, relating to short forms of conveyances and mortgages, which is given a peculiar statutory efficacy, to the recitals. Notwithstanding the new law enunciated tonight by the Minister of National Defence, that the recitals control the construction of a
document, I desire to say that the draftsman who wrote these recitals had a good deal of impudence. What did he do? He made Sir William Petersen agree that he understood about the conditions of the agricultural, manufacturing and industrial people of this country; and he made Sir William Petersen say that there was a combine. Here is a man who, no doubt, has been dealing with the alleged combine at one time or another saying, "It is in the interests of Canada that this thing should be done; there are combines, I know it, and therefore I agree with these recitals." These recitals, which have nothing whatever to do with the agreement, occupy about one-fourth of it. Consequently I was naturally prejudiced against the document because I knew there was propaganda in it. It goes forth with the blazing sanction apparently of a Supreme court judge, and then there is this propaganda of the recitals. Last night the Prime Minister asked':	"What is the reason
of the propaganda that has been undertaken by the steamship companies in opposition to this agreement? How fearful they are," he said, "of the great damage to be done to them by this David's pebble that we are throwing into their ranks!" They had to answer the propaganda in this agreement, published daily throughout the country; they had to answer the Preston alleged case; and they would not have been self-respecting men unless they had done so. Anything that has appeared' in the newspapers or otherwise from the shipping interests has been to give the lie to the Preston report and to contradict the propaganda which the government itself has placed in the agreement and broadcasted so widely. I want to say at the outset that if there is any possible way of getting cheaper transportation rates on the ocean, on the land or in the air, I am all for it. No member of this House can be of stronger mind in that respect than I am, and I believe that is the attitude of this section of the House. It is absolutely unfair to impute that we are standing for the maintenance of a combine which is not in the interests of the people.
In passing, I am interested to revert to about twenty years ago, when, a government being in power in Ontario adverse to the party to which I have always belonged, and there being in charge of the administration of justice at Ottawa a minister of the party of the Prime Minister, a prosecution was undertaken, called the Plumbers' Supply Case, in which I happened to play a part. Men who were engaged in the supply of plumbers' goods were charged under, I believe, section 496 of the criminal code with forming an improper combine. The case
Ocean Shipping Rates

was heard by the late Mr. Justice Clute, and in the course of the testimony it developed that the combination was distinctly in the interests of everyone who had anything to do with the supply and use of plumbers' goods. Two of the men charged were found guilty; they practically admitted the charge; they were fined. The case was taken up with the Liberal government, and they said, " Here, this is striking where the blow should not be struck, this combine is in the interests of the people of this province;" and no further prosecution followed.
Coming to the agreement itself, as I say, I was led to examine it narrowly; and notwithstanding what the Minister of National Defence has just said, implying that you might get an agreement which lawyers might determine one way, but if they lived down by the sea where he does, or if it dealt with shipping, they would find that they were mistaken and that what they would naturally expect to follow from the words used did not follow but that the words had some other cryptic and unexpected meaning;-I say, Mr. Speaker,

and I would not assert it unless I absolutely believed it, and I am sure it would not do me very much good professionally, otherwise-that this contract has not only one " joker " but half a dozen or more, and that these " jokers " are inserted for the purpose of withdrawing from the attention of the public and of this House the actual effect of the agreement itself. I do not wish to cover the ground that was traversed this afternoon, but section 1 of the contract permits of its assignment to any German, United States or other foreign company. The draftsman protecting the high contracting party, might very well have said that the assignment should be approved of by the minister. The minister ought to know, this government ought to know, the House ought to know, the country ought to know *who are the people getting the money that the country is paying. Section (a) of clause 1 has been read before; it provides:
That the contractor shall build, equip, provide, establish and during this contract continue and, in the manner hereinafter mentioned, operate a regular shipping service between the ports designated.
I submit that there is no question at all about the legal interpretation of the phrase,
" operate a regular shipping service." The duty is placed upon the contractor of establishing the service; he therefore can say what it is to be; afterwards he operates it. What does " regular '' mean? I submit it is simply grotesque to say that it bears the meaning given to it by the Minister of National Defence. His words were, " A regular shipping

service is a continuous service throughout the year." I w'onder if those who pay their rent regularly on the first of the month think the " regular " part of it is a continuous payment and not a payment at fixed monthly intervals. The judicial meaning-and there will be no trouble to satisfy even the Minister of National Defence upon this-the judicial meaning of "regular" is "recurring or repeated at fixed times.". And it is true in the case of any service contract, as the minister can be well assured. That being so, the duty falls upon Petersen of establishing a shipping service, operating at certain recurring intervals, and when he has done that he has fulfilled the requirements imposed upon him by section (a) of clause 1. If he decides to give a monthly service, can anyone deny him the right to do so? Can the government say, "Oh, we expected a weekly service?" Petersen's answer would be: "I am very sorry, but you entered into a contract with me under which I was to establish and operate a regular shipping service. The shipping service that I have decided to establish is a monthly service. If you wanted anything else you should have stipulated for it; as you did not stipulate for it, and the duty being given me under the contract of establishing it, I am entitled to establish a service with such recurring periods as I see fit. That is my full duty under the contract, and that is all you will get." And if the government try to get back at him by saying that he may not use his boats in any other service, Petersen's answer will be: "You did not provide that I should not engage in any other service I have established that regular service and when I am not on that service I can do anything I like except work for the combine. I can charge whatever I like. I am independent of the combine; I can ply my boats in other services, get the avails from them and put them in my pocket, and you cannot say one word about it." What answer could the government make in a court of justice to a claim made by Petersen in this connection? The Prime Minister says that not five cents will go to Petersen until he fulfils the terms of his contract; that payment is after performance. But when Petersen establishes that monthly service, at the expiration of the very first month he is entitled to demand from the government the full amount of the monthly subsidy, and if the government does not pay it to him he can take his case into court and recover the money. It would have been easy to add at the end of section (a) a clause something to this effect:

Ocean Shipping Rates
-and the ships engaged in such service shall be engaged in no other service without the consent of the minister.
But that was not done. In the next place we come to clause (d). I really must repeat this, for the sake of emphasis:
That the control and regulation of the rates to be charged by the contractor shall rest with the government of Canada and that the government shall fix transportation rates on all commodities from time to time.
I submit that whoever was looking after the interests of the crown might have added something to this effect:
-and the contractor shall carry all freight offered at the said fixed rates, provided always that he has cargo space available therefor.
There is a provision that the control of rates is with the government; they are to fix prices. But. if in a bookstore the price of a book is fixed, I need not buy at that price; I can say: "I will pay so much less and you can take it or leave it," So in this case: I can employ myself on other services; it is not a hardship to me if I decline to carry at the rate you fix. If the rate is fixed at such an amount that Petersen does not want to carry, then he can decline to carry and the government will not get the service. The farmers may be clamouring for shipment of their wheat, and the government is compelled to go to Petersen and say: "We are paying you a big subsidy; we want you to carry this wheat." Petersen says, "I am not going to carry it at the price you fixed." The government may then ask at what price he will carry it, and Petersen will say: "If the government want their commodities carried they must pay me my price, otherwise the carrying will not be done." So in such cases the subsidy will be earned although the goods are not carried.
The effect of clause 3 of the agreement is to give Petersen the benefit of the maintenance of a service in excess of ten ships if he wants to establish it. The government has no control over the number of ships that he may put in the service. The contract says:
The subsidy aforementioned shall be increased or reduced as the case may be in proportion to the number of ships operated and maintained by the contractor in the service aforesaid from time to time and such increase or reduction of subsidy shall be added to or deducted from the monthly payments hereinbefore provided for in paragraph two.
You will note that Petersen is given the right, by clause 3, to increase, whereas in clause 6 the government is given the right to increase. It is important, in the interpretation of these two clauses, to remember that the provision as to the subsidy is twice stated. If it does not mean that Petersen is to have the right to increase, with an increased subsidy,
and that the government is to have the right to increase, under clause 6, with an increased subsidy, then the repetition of the provision as to subsidy is the worst kind of bad draftsmanship. It is a mere vain repetition; it has no purpose at all in the document.
As to clause 4, I wish merely to refer to two expressions. It says, "shipping services to be established by the contractor." That is the only place in the contract where the plural "services" is used. These services are to be established by the contractor, and following, as it does, clause 3-and, I submit, in explanation of and consonant with it- Petersen has the right, even against the expressed wish of the government, to increase the number of ships he has under subsidy. The word "loyally" is not a word of airt when used in an agreement of this kind. The draftsman might just as well have used the word "righteously," or "warmly" or any other expression of that kind.
The Prime Minister declared in his speech that the government had the right to say what commodities the contractor should carry. Then why insert clause 7, wherein the right of the contractor to carry nitro-glycerine is negatived? Clause 9 merely says that any voyages Petersen undertakes, in the supposed ease of the establishing of a regular shipping service of one 'boat a month, shall be prosecuted with "all possible speed and despatch."
Now, Mr. Speaker, a sad comment upon this agreement is found in the agreement of 1897 between this same gentleman and the then government,. That agreement is' found in volume 2 of the Debates of the House of Commons, of the session of 1897. Whole clauses are picked out of the 1897 contract and inserted in this agreement, but whoever was acting for the government took very good care that the clauses which would place a burden on Petersen were not taken out of that old contract and inserted in this agreement.
Let us see what the agreement of 1897 provided. It provided that the service was to be a fast weekly service. First of all, there was to be a fortnightly service, then a weekly service, and when the fortnightly service was instituted, one-half of the subsidy that the weekly service would afterwards claim was given. The terms and conditions as to carriage were to be "as the Governor in Counoil deems expedient;" that is left out of this agreement. The days and times of sailing were subject to the approval of the minister; that is left out of this agreement. The minister reserved the right, on notice, to change the time of sailing; that is left out of this agreement. The 1897 agree-

I would say that it is taking money out of the pockets of the people of the country and putting it into the pockets of Petersen without any benefit to the country. I would apply to this resolution the words used by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in relation to the amendment.. And while he dharacterized the interpretation put upon the contract by my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) as 'wholly inaccurate and absurd, I think we are entitled to have an expression of opinion from someone not connected with the government, not connected with any party in this House, who will give a disinterested view of the merits of the question and state exactly what the contract really means. I am satisfied as to what the result would be if such an opinion were asked. This resolution says that to give the government of Canada control over certain ocean rates "it is expedient", and so on. maintopic: EARNINGS FROM A "PETERSEN" STEAMER VOYAGE IN THE SEASON 1924 (AS PUBLISHED IN "HANSARD" PAGE 723) COMPARED WITH EARNINGS BASED UPON THE AVERAGE FREIGHT RATES FOR 1913 FROM MONTREAL TO LONDON
speechtext:
Let me at the outset make mj' position clear so far as the combine is concerned. I have never had any doubt., from the first time I had an opportunity of learning anything about steamship rates, that a combine has existed, and possibly because I happen to belong to a class that is accustomed to exploitation by all and everybody, I came to the conclusion that it was a pernicious combine. And I still believe it to be pernicious. I do not think it is in the interests of trade, or agriculture, of business generally, that the control of rates should be in the hands of private individuals, any more than I believe that the control of public credit should be a private affair. Nor have I heard any hon. gentleman in this House so far urge that a combine does not exist. Some may have inferred that from utterances in the course of heated debate, but I have not heard anyone yet dispute the fact. Anyone who would do that has hardly given the subject the study which the resolution now before the House must have suggested to him.
I find that a combine has existed on the north Atlantic for something like fifty years, commencing about the time steam was replacing sail. At that time rates began to rise and they have risen fairly steadily ever since. Investigations have been numerous, joint inquiries have been held, but in all the inquiries that I have looked into I have failed to find any single one that W'as carried to a satisfactory conclusion. I do not think this country has ever entered with Great Britain or any other country into a joint conference on these matters and come to a conclusive decision as to wdiat was the best method of controlling rates. I think that something along that line should be done; we should at any rate make the attempt. I will come to that phase of the discussion a little later.
The recent renewal of investigations has simply cast light on a subject that had become shadowed because of the lack of public interest in it. Economic conditions becoming oppressively burdensome on the people, we began to hunt around for the various causes of trouble; and so in the committee on Agricultural Conditions which sat in 1923, and of which my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. Mc-Master) was so distinguished and ornamental a chairman, a glaring light was thrown upon the existence of this North Atlantic combine. The subject had also been referred to either in 1920 or 1921 when, before a special committee of this House investigating the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, Mr. Teakle was examined. As hon. members know, Mr. 132S
Ocean Shipping Rates

Teakle was the general manager of the merchant marine, and in answer to a question put to him by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) he admitted the existence of a rate conference in Montreal on which representatives of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine were sitting in. We heard no more about the matter until 1923. I find, looking further back, that the Board of Trade of Great Britain had investigated this subject in 1910 when they submitted a report, the material part of which has been referred to by hon. members to my right, as well as by the Minister of Railways, and been placed on Hansard. That report was to the effect that a combine existed, and that it was advisable that there should be a joint inquiry with Canada in regard to it. In 1913 the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) , then chairman of the railway commission, was sent to Great Britain and in view of the conclusions arrived at by the Board of Trade he suggested that a joint inquiry was advisable. He attempted to have such an inquiry set on foot. It was discovered however that there was in existence a body known as the Dominions Royal Commission which I believe was investigating somewhere around New Zealand and which was expected shortly to be in Canada. He interviewed the chairman of that commission who happened to be in England, and he recommended that if the commission intended taking up the subject of a transAtlantic conference the matter could not be left in better hands. It may be noted that even at that time it was admitted that large increases in rates had taken place and that, as well, there had been a falling off in the rate of imports from Great Britain to Canada. The investigation suggested was not to be confined to the freight situation but was also to take up the whole question of passenger rates. The hon. member for West York was not successful in securing this joint inquiry for the reason I have stated. He did on his own account investigate matters to some extent and he made a very comprehensive report to the Board of Railway Commissioners on his return. The following action taken by him I only know from information through other people. Now let me point out to the House that I have never been a friend of the Tory party, and I hope I never will be a political friend of the Tory party, I have no intention I assure you, of ever allying myself with a party with the reputation and characteristics which that party has. But let me in fairness say that in my opinion Sir Henry Drayton brought back an infinitely fairer and more comprehensive 
report, and did more in England at that time, to remove combine evils than the recent delegate of this government did when ;he was in that country. At that time there existed two great evils of the combine, the children of the system. One was the " fighting ship " and the other was the deferred rebates clause called the "loyalty clause." Whether it was the result wholly of Sir Henry Drayton's intervention or not I am not sure and have not been able to ascertain. I know the United States was conducting an inquiry at that time into the same matters; but it is enough for us to know that during the year in which Stir Henry Drayton reported to Canada those two great evils were removed so far as North Atlantic conferences were concerned. What was this " fighting ship "? It was sort of privateer, especially built for the service required of it, that of competing with any lines on trade routes on which non- conference ships were operating with the effect that the non-conference 'line of ships was either driven out of business or forced into the combine. That was a most unfair form of competition. That is gone. At least no trace of it was found by the chairman of the Agricultural Conditions committee in 1923. The "loyalty clause" was simply an arrangement with the shipper that if he would give all his business to a conference boat, it did not matter which line of boats, provided the boat was in the conference, he received a ten per cent rebate of the cost. That was regarded as a most unjust and unfair form of competition and in restraint of trade. Those two evils have been removed so far as the north Atlantic is concerned.
The report we have before us, and upon which undoubtedly public opinion is expected to develop in support of the subsidy, is of little value. Everything that is in it that is material to the case was discovered by the special committee on Agricultural Conditions, and indeed by previous investigations. I wonder why the government appointed Mr. Preston. I know nothing about him. I have nothing to say about his character. I know nothing of his political career, but the question occurred to me as a fair and impartial examiner of this matter, why appoint Mr. Preston? Were there not plenty of qualified men within the ranks of our own civil servants, men who had experience, men in the Trade and Commerce department, in the Customs and Excise department, in the Department of Marine and Fisheries, men in various other departments, who had technical knowledge, and whose time was being paid for in any case? I have never heard any hon. gentlemen

Ocean Shipping Rates
opposite explain why it was necessary to go outside the service, and by so doing hand the plum to an outsider, which plum undoubtedly would have helped to stimulate the brain and the initiative of members of the civil service itself. Not only that, but I submit in passing that it would have accorded much better with the avowed policy of economy on the part of this government had it made an appointment from the civil service.
As far as the report itself is concerned, I cannot afford to waste much time on it, for the reason that has already been stated quite frequently that the recommendation of the government is not based upon that report, but that it is based upon the report made by my hon. friend the chairman of the Agricultural Conditions committee. Let us therefore consider the contract itself, and although I cannot attempt to give it the deep legal examination that hon. members to my right have given it, I can view it in the light of the ordinary man of the street, the business man. Ten small boats are going to be used by this government to control rates. I want hon. members now to imagine the export trade of Canada, a huge trade, then to imagine the capacity of ten boats, and ask themselves this question, how much of the total trade of Canada can ten boats carry? Certainly a very small proportion of it. How much of any single commodity can ten boats carry? Probably a large quantity of any single commodity. But the government may set rates till it is black in the face, and it cannot fix the rate for traffic unless it can establish competition. There is no use whatever in the government stating that this contract is to enable the government to control rates. The government cannot control rates unless it controls enough space to handle sufficient of each of the commodities shipped from Canada to create competition in the rates charged on those commodities. I hope that is clear, because I want to be fair in this matter. I welcome an interruption at any time, if I am not fair.

speechtext:
There is one other point that occurs to me as a result of the interruption. The subsidy is to be paid annually, we presume, for ten years-SI,350,-000. But we will assume that one or two more boats are added and that we are paying two million dollars per year for ten years, making twenty million dollars; and at the end of ten years we decide to stop the subsidy-where are we? We have spent twenty million dollars, and Mr. Combine rears his head as strong or stronger than ever before- at the end of ten years of experimentation and an expenditure of twenty million dollars. It is ridiculous for hon. gentlemen in any part of the House to talk about smashing the combine. Combines cannot be smashed. They can be absorbed but cannot be smashed. Under the present competitive commercial system, a combine is a natural growth, and things that are natural cannot be destroyed even by subsidies. Now imagine the situation: Here is a combine. To what extent it would control rates even I have no power to demonstrate to this House. But I will use the words of Mr. Preston himself:
The North Atlantic steamship combine is only one section of the steamship conference now endeavouring to control all the great shipping interests of the world. . . . The object in all cases is the same. It is not unreasonable to infer that it is the control of the ocean commerce of the world, fixing freight and passenger rates solely in the interest of those controlling the vast tonnage and shipping traversing these waterways.
And ten boats of moderate tonnage are setting out to smash a combine with all those interlocking interests powerfully supporting it on every hand. The thing does not appeal to me as being reasonable. I am anxious that control of rates be established. I do not think any hon. gentleman in this House is not. I would desire to see effective rate control established to-morrow, and if I thought for one instant that this subsidy would give effective control of rates in the interest of all Canada, I would even overcome my natural instinct against subsidies and support the government on it.

maintopic: EARNINGS FROM A "PETERSEN" STEAMER VOYAGE IN THE SEASON 1924 (AS PUBLISHED IN "HANSARD" PAGE 723) COMPARED WITH EARNINGS BASED UPON THE AVERAGE FREIGHT RATES FOR 1913 FROM MONTREAL TO LONDON
speechtext:
I will come to that a little later if the hon: gentleman is patient. It is ridiculous to talk of smashing a combine of this size by creating a competitive system with a subsidy and ten small
Ocean Shipping Rates

boats, very ordinary boats, indeed. A moment ago I asked a question: Who was going to benefit? We have to export annually from Canada overseas, principally by the Atlantic ocean, an enormous quantity of grain and a fairly large number of cattle, so far as the agricultural population is concerned. I am going to make this a sectional matter for just a moment, because hon. members opposite have turned their faces to this corner of the House and made appeals to us on the ground that this would help agriculture, help the cattle business, help the grain business, and hon. members to my right have attempted to show us that it would not help either of these. Wheat is out of the conference altogether. It is subject to competition, so subject to it that the fluctuations in cargo space for wheat are very striking. An examination of the rates during last year will reveal a spread of all the way from nothing to thirty-four or thirty-five cents a bushel. Thirty-five cents, I think, was the limit. The Prime Minister states that he is going to control all rates. I want to ask him if it is his intention to control the rate on wheat. If it is, I want to register my unalterable opposition to his so doing, unless it be a maximum rate subject to fluctuations below. What would be the situation we would be in? We would be in much the situation that we suspect we are in as regards the railway commission at the present time. We have a strong suspicion that rates on grain should be lower but are not lower because the rates on other commodities must be low. If this government control of steamship cargo rates is going to involve also the control of rates on wheat, in other words to take the wheat rates out of competition and place them at some lined level, I regard that as a most sinister proposal. Let me call the attention of the government to the remarks of Mr. Preston on this very matter, at page 22 of his report:
The fluctuation in the cost of transporting wheat between Montreal and Liverpool may be seen in the following schedule, compiled from reports published by the Dominion Statistical Bureau.
Note the following:
The range of freight charges on wheat from five cents to thirty-five cents per bushel offers a problem to which profitable consideration may be given, if possible, of securing more stable freight rates.
The whole report was written with a view to breaking the stable freight rates of the combine and creating competitive rates, and Mr. Preston suggests in this part of it that wheat and wheat alone should be subject to stable rates. I do not like the look of it, and if the government proposes to fix wheat rates and by raising, even a little, the average price for transporting wheat to Liverpool or any-

where else, in order to afford lower rates on other commodities, I am absolutely opposed to it.
Let us take the cattle situation just for a moment. I find that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company were invited to handle cattle, and they refused to do so on the ground that the traffic was not profitable. We are told, however, that the traffic must be profitable because the rates are so high. That may be true, 'but I have not yet, nor has the committee on Agricultural Conditions-and I hope my hon. friend (Mr. McMaster) will correct me if I am incorrect-received information that cattle rates are exorbitant. That they are too high for the business, I admit, but that the steamship lines are charging exorbitant rates on cattle has not yet been proved. If any hon. member wishes to dispute the statement, I await the disputation. If not, we will proceed. The Canadian Pacific will not handle the business at all and does not want to. We will presume there is no money in that business for the Canadian Pacific. I will take the report of the select standing committee on National Railways and Shipping of last year, and I will ask hon. members to look at pages 8 and 9 where Sir Henry Thornton is being examined:
By Mr. Jelliff: Q. That does not cause you any additional expense?
That is referring to the tearing out of any structures for the transportation of cattle.
A. No. Now, to go on with these various items of expense. Simmered down it amounts to this; it makes the cost of carriage per head $17.48. and the revenue per head at the present rate is $20, leaving a profit to the company of $2.52 per head.
That is Sir Henry Thornton's evidence last year.
Bv Sir Henry Drayton: Q. Does that include all the items you have mentioned?-A. Yes.
Q. And does that include a fair proportion of the fuel and other expenses of the voyage?-A. No, it is the bare cost of handling the cattle. We have not charged anything for operating the ships against these cattle. Perhaps we should.
Q. It really puts itself in this position, that the difference between $17.48 and $20 will apply on the general cost of running the boat?-A. That is it.
Q. And you find out afterwards whether you have made a profit or a loss?
Hon. gentlemen will note this answer by Sir Henry Thornton:
A. It does not require a very wide flight of the imagination to see what happens, especially if you charged interest on the cost of the vessel. While 1 do not want anything that I say to be misinterpreted as an effort in the direction of propaganda for increasing cattle receipts, at the same time, generally speaking, $20 per head on cattle to the United Kingdom is not considered a high charge in the shipping world.

Ocean Shipping Kates
When we have evidence of that kind before us. we wonder at the temerity of hon. members who appeal to us, almost plead with us to support this subsidy 'because it will reduce, they say, the rate on cattle ten dollars per head. In the first place, last year we exported about 63,000 head of cattle. Only ten boats would be handling this traffic and they can carry only a limited number of cattle, about 500 on an average per boat.

July, August and September are the better months. If we can get the cattle off then, what do we hit? Another reason that I offer is that Mr. Petersen cannot handle our cattle. He is going to have to handle 63.000 cattle in three months. Why do I say that? Because, Mr. Speaker, if he has to handle our cattle at a loss- and he will have to if Sir Henry Thornton is to be believed-then he will have to handle all the traffic, because nobody else will handle any of it. That must be obvious. If he is go:ng to handle all of it, then the government will have to undertake another responsibility- the responsibility of orderly organizing the coming forward of the cattle so that they will reach the boats at the proper time to be shipped and in proper condition. speechtext: Will my hon. friend permit me right there? The Canadian Pacific Railway Company got a charter from the Dominion parliament, under certain terms and conditions, to do certain things.
