speechtext: I have not contended otherwise, Mr. Speaker-not yet; I may before I get through. Up to the present all I have suggested is that the government might have gone to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company before approaching Sir William Petersen and tried to come to some terms with that company, which, after all is largely our own. Hon. members have often referred to it in glowing terms as one of the great assets of Canada, a splendid thing, a thing of which we should be proud.

maintopic: EARNINGS FROM A "PETERSEN" STEAMER VOYAGE IN THE SEASON 1924 (AS PUBLISHED IN "HANSARD" PAGE 723) COMPARED WITH EARNINGS BASED UPON THE AVERAGE FREIGHT RATES FOR 1913 FROM MONTREAL TO LONDON
speechtext:
Would my hon. friend
confiscate the property of any person or any corporation which has obtained certain rights from the federal parliament or from any legislature of this country? If the government of Canada want to make an agreement have they not the right to go to any firm or corporation they wish? If they do not go to the people that my hon. friend thinks they should go to, then is there any reason why those people should be compelled by act of a legislature or of this parliament to enter into such an agreement? In other words, does the hon. member approve of the principle of holding the big stick over people who have charters from the parliament of this country7?

maintopic: EARNINGS FROM A "PETERSEN" STEAMER VOYAGE IN THE SEASON 1924 (AS PUBLISHED IN "HANSARD" PAGE 723) COMPARED WITH EARNINGS BASED UPON THE AVERAGE FREIGHT RATES FOR 1913 FROM MONTREAL TO LONDON
speechtext:
I would
ask my7 hon. friend to be so good as to allow me to dissect the several questions he has put, and to reply to them to-morrow. I could not hope to answer them to-night, and all at once.
The Prime Minister in the early stages of his speech the other day said, referring, to the resolution before the House:
The resolution is the first necessary step to be taken by the government preliminary to the introduction of a bill to give the government control of ocean rates. The
Ocean Shipping Rates

resolution relates to the control of ocean rates; that is the principle underlying it, and lion, members in voting upon the resolution are passing on the important question whether or not in their opinion the government should undertake to control ocean rates. Whether the method which the government is taking to control ocean rates may be effective or not is a subject which,
I think admits of debate.
I think so; I will agree with the Prime Minister there. There is no doubt about it; but if it does admit of debate, of discussion, of alteration, or possibly of total elimination, why are we asked now to vote upon it? The Prime Minister says we are simply voting on the question of control. If I could convince myself that that was all we were voting on, I should be only too pleased to vote with the government. But this House is governed by certain rules

and mind you, I think a good many of those rules could be amended. I do not like some of them-they hamper us; they are restrictive from the point of view of modern business methods. For example, there is one rule that prevents me from expressing my real opinion on this matter.
As I understand it, the motion before the House is that the Speaker do now leave the chair for the House to resolve itself into committee of the Whole on a certain resolution. The amendment before the House is that the Speaker do not now leave the chair but that the House resolve itself-and so on; I need not quote that. Frankly, with all kindness to my friends to my right, I do not think they have 'been very constructive. I do not think there is anything in the amendment which I could support, with the exception, and this is my personal opinion, on the evidence so far produced, that this report of Mr. Preston's and the policy of the government are ill advised, costly and futile. To that extent I can agree with the amendment. But as to the proposal which it offers, cooperation in joint inquiry with other portions of the empire-well, I hate to think that we lack sufficient intelligence to find a solution before such a conference could decide upon the subject. So that so far as the amendment is concerned I am, afraid I shall have to vote against it.
As to the motion itself, what does it say? That the Speaker do now leave the chair for the House to resolve itself into committee of the Whole on this resolution-and I will ask hon. members to listen to the opening words of the resolution:
Resolved, that to give the government of Canada control over certain ocean rates it is expedient to ratify and confirm the agrement between His Majesty and Sir William Petersen.
If the resolution simply read:

Resolved, that to give the government of Canada control over certain ocean rates it is expedient that this whole question should be referred to a select standing committee for consideration and recommendation-
-then we could vote for it. But it goes further than that; it states specifically that the control which the government says it wants to secure is control by virtue of an agreement between this government and Sir William Petersen. Now the Prime Minister, whose kindness in the matter I appreciate, told us that we did not necessarily bind ourselves to the subsidy in voting for the resolution. I cannot for the life of me see how he can excuse us from voting for the subsidy if we vote for the resolution, and if any hon. gentleman opposite speaks after me I will be very glad indeed if he would release my mind from this understanding, because I would be only too willing to support the government in further prosecuting their investigations in the hope of arriving at a solution. But as it stands I am hampered. Suppose we accept his statement, that this is a motion that the House now resolve itself into committee of the Whole. Once we get into committee of the Whole, where are we? We are in a trap absolutely, those of us who do not think this is a practical proposal, those of us who are opposed to subsidies in principle. We are in a trap which can only be opened for our escape by the government itself. And what is the trap? The trap is this, that the second reading of the resolution determines the principle of the resolution; that is as I understand it. The second reading of the resolution w'hen passed carries the principle of the resolution forward into the bill, which will be brought down later, and is again concurred in. True, I may oppose it in committee; I may vote against it, but the vote is not recorded; it is simply a counted vote. Effective opposition to the proposal can hardly come in committee of the Whole.
There is one suggestion I have to .make to the Prime Minister, and I do so with all kindness because I am anxious to support him in his investigation into this whole question of control. Will the Prime Minister or will the government make this offer to us? Will he give me an undertaking that the following will be his attitude? That if we go into committee of the Whole this question will not be pressed to a second reading of the resolution in committee of the Whole, when the principle would be determined, but that the government will after a certain formal debate has taken place, move that the debate be adjourned? Then we will find on the order paper next day Item No. 16 or Item No. 18, or whatever it may be, "House again

Ocean Shipping Rates
in committee of the Whole on a certain resolution". Next day the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce could rise in his place and move that that item be struck from the order paper, and that this whole question be referred to a special committee. I offer that to the government as a solution, as a way out of its dilemma and a way out of ours. I am anxious to support the government, but I cannot tie myself to the principle of this hopelessly futile subsidy to ten small ships.
Were I permitted to move an amendment to the amendment, were I even permitted to move an amendment after the amendment now before us had been disposed of, I would move one in terms not dissimilar to this:
That Mr. Speaker do not now leave the chair, but that it be resolved:
That it is advisable that a select special committee be appointed to make inquiry into the question of steamship transportation, it having been alleged that a combine exists known as the North Atlantic Conference ; and
That it is advisable to afford opportunity to all interested parties to submit their view's upon the subject matter of the inquiry to the said committee, with particular regard to the possibility of discovering the best method for effectively controlling steamship rates by the Dominion of Canada;
And that the said committee shall have power to send for persons, papers and records including what minutes and evidence and reports of previous investigations may be considered necessary, and to examine witnesses under oath and to report from time to time.
That, Mr. Speaker, would be my amendment if I had the power to move it. I have not the power to move it now under the rules. I do not wish to embarrass the government. I wish to co-operate with them in this matter, and I cannot move it very well on second reading of the resolution without embarrassing them further. I ask now, if the government are honestly anxious to arrive at a solution of this problem, that they either take this step or any other that appeals to them that may save themselves and ourselves from the position in , which we find ourselves, and refer the whole matter to a committee. I am quite sure many hon. members on the other side of the House-I look at the hon. member for Brome (Mr. Mc-Master), I look at the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler)-and many others who would be only too delighted to see some such solution of this question put forward by the government. I make this suggestion with the sincere desire to cooperate with the government.
Before I take my seat I wish to express my regret that when the Prime Minister was speaking he did not read the whole of the report of the special committee on Agricultural Conditions. I also must take this opportunity of telling my hon. friend from 86
South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) that he was incorrect and unfair when he said that the special committee had reported without discussion.

maintopic: EARNINGS FROM A "PETERSEN" STEAMER VOYAGE IN THE SEASON 1924 (AS PUBLISHED IN "HANSARD" PAGE 723) COMPARED WITH EARNINGS BASED UPON THE AVERAGE FREIGHT RATES FOR 1913 FROM MONTREAL TO LONDON
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will permit me, I am sure he does not wish to misrepresent me. I think I made it perfectly clear in speaking on this motion that I did not censure the committee in any way.
I merely pointed out that in so far as I was concerned I had not heard the report, and I was not present when it was passed.
As far as the question put to the Prime Minister was concerned, I still think there is an error in the report of what I said. If you will compare it with the words I used in speaking on this motion, you will find that I made it perfectly clear that this report of the committee was passed on one morning several weeks after the evidence had been submitted to it, that I was not present at the committee meeting, that I had not heard the report read, and did not know anything about it until after parliament had prorogued.

maintopic: EARNINGS FROM A "PETERSEN" STEAMER VOYAGE IN THE SEASON 1924 (AS PUBLISHED IN "HANSARD" PAGE 723) COMPARED WITH EARNINGS BASED UPON THE AVERAGE FREIGHT RATES FOR 1913 FROM MONTREAL TO LONDON
speechtext:
I am quite willing to accept the hon. gentleman's explanation, but the fact of the matter is that an impression was left upon the House to the effect that the special committee had hurriedly jammed through their report without discussion. There is no doubt that was the impression left. Now in fairness to the chairman of that committee, who in my opinion is one of the fairest minded men in the House of Commons, I wish to quote from the report of the committee, at page lvi: This report is dated Wednesday, June 13, 1923. I quote:
Chairman submitted to committee for approval a suggested further report to the House on ocean freight rates. After discussion of same, clerk was ordered to have sufficient copies typed forthwith to supply each member of the committee with a copy.
Again on Friday, June 15, 1923, I find this:
The fifth interim report-that of ocean freight rates -was again taken up and discussed, and laid over until the next meeting of the committee.
Again on Monday, June 18, 1923, I find:
Chairman read redraft of proposed report to the House on ocean transportation.
Discussion followed.
On motion of Mr. Caldwell, seconded by Mr. Munro, the draft report as read by the chairman was adopted, and the chairman ordered to present it to the House as the fifth interim report of this committee.
I do not put this on record in any carping spirit of criticism, nor with any desire to reflect upon the hon. member for South Oxford, but simply because my impression and the impression, that others who heard him speak gathered from his remarks was that no discussion had taken place on the report. I do

Ocean Shipping Rates

not think it was the hon. member's intention to create that impression.

maintopic: EARNINGS FROM A "PETERSEN" STEAMER VOYAGE IN THE SEASON 1924 (AS PUBLISHED IN "HANSARD" PAGE 723) COMPARED WITH EARNINGS BASED UPON THE AVERAGE FREIGHT RATES FOR 1913 FROM MONTREAL TO LONDON
speechtext: I attempted to point out while the Prime Minister was speaking that the report of this committee was not read when it was submitted to the House, and consequently the members were not familiar with it. When I spoke on this motion, I made it perfectly clear that the chairman of the committee had done everything possible to get all the evidence that was available and I asked the Prime Minister to read the seventh and final report which indicated that owing to inability to digest the evidence taken it was advisable to have the committee reappointed.

maintopic: EARNINGS FROM A "PETERSEN" STEAMER VOYAGE IN THE SEASON 1924 (AS PUBLISHED IN "HANSARD" PAGE 723) COMPARED WITH EARNINGS BASED UPON THE AVERAGE FREIGHT RATES FOR 1913 FROM MONTREAL TO LONDON
speechtext:
The Prime Minister referred to this report of the special committee on Agricultural Conditions and he quoted at some length from Mr. Lubin and other witnesses. But he did not quote all; let me quote some more that he might have referred to. At >page 20 the following appears:
The question of ocean freight is a world problem and one of very great importance to all countries. As a world problem it cannot be settled satisfactorily by any one nation nor by any one interest acting alone.
Mr. Lubin was then quoting from Mr. Hippwood, the assistant secretary of the Marine department. He goes on to quote Mr. Alexander, the chairman of the committee of the House of Representatives on merchant marine matters:
It is true that our government would be impotent to enforce reasonable rates or stabilize rates on farm products in international trade in the absence of an international agreement. It is an international problem and can only be solved by international agreement.
I wish the Prime Minister had not left these quotations out.

maintopic: EARNINGS FROM A "PETERSEN" STEAMER VOYAGE IN THE SEASON 1924 (AS PUBLISHED IN "HANSARD" PAGE 723) COMPARED WITH EARNINGS BASED UPON THE AVERAGE FREIGHT RATES FOR 1913 FROM MONTREAL TO LONDON
speechtext:
Why not vote for the
amendment then?

maintopic: EARNINGS FROM A "PETERSEN" STEAMER VOYAGE IN THE SEASON 1924 (AS PUBLISHED IN "HANSARD" PAGE 723) COMPARED WITH EARNINGS BASED UPON THE AVERAGE FREIGHT RATES FOR 1913 FROM MONTREAL TO LONDON
speechtext:
We come now to page 21, where we find that the committee reported as follows. Part of this has been already put on Hansard, but it is so important as to warrant repetition by way of emphasis:
Your committee, in view of the foregoing and of the evidence adduced before them and referred to in a previous interim report, are of the opinion that action is desirable to control shipping rings or conferences.
It is suggested that the Canadian representatives in attendance at the next meeting of the International Institute of Agriculture should be given authority to see that the matter is thoroughly discussed, in order to discover whether an international system of control is feasible through such agency.
In view of the fact that a very great deal of the shipping coming to Canadian ports is British shipping concurrent action by the British authorities is respectfully suggested. The matter might well be made a subject for discussion and consideration at the ner.t Imperial Economic Conference.

Meanwhile it would appear wise to recommend that the government through one of its departments-we suggest the Department of Trade and Commerce-should entertain complaints from shippers of unfair or oppressive treatment by ocean carriers and should hold investigations publicly or privately into such complaints.
This last recommendation is the only part of the report which the government would appear to have carried out; the government certainly has entertained complaints of all kinds from every one in the matter and I congratulate them in that respect. At the bottom of the page we find the following:
The Canadian people are the owners of 67 ships. Some of these are of fair though not large size. Your committee suggest that a certain number of these ships might be selected to be operated in conjunction with our National railway lines, that the freight rates on such steamers could be established on the cost of carriage plus a reasonable profit based upon the real, as opposed to the cost, value of the ships. If these ships are of the size and type which can be economically and efficiently run in conjunction with the National railways (and on these points your committee have taken no evidence) the following desirable objects would be obtained. The National Railways would be enabled to grant through bills of lading on a transportation system by land and by water altogether under their own control; the Canadian people would be able to obtain transportation facilities at reasonable and known rates; the service thus given on the ocean would tend to maintain rates on a reasonable basis and would act as a deterrent to the charging of unreasonable rates by other lines; and finally the knowledge obtained by the government as to the actual cost of ocean transportation would aid it in determining whether rates charged by other lines are fair and reasonable.
Should it appear-
And it was really amusing to me, Mr. Speaker, to hear the Minister of National Defence quote this.
Should it appear that there are no ships or not a sufficient number of ships belonging to the Canadian Government Merchant Marine suitable for this service then it would appear that wisdom would dictate the disposal of some of the smaller ships to enable ships of the class required to be secured.
I have asked several of the members of the committee the meaning of that sentence in the report and there is no question as to what it signifies. If these boats were too small for the service or were not efficient, the suggestion was that they should be sold and that other boats, government owned, should be purchased in their stead.
Now let me offer a suggestion as a constructive proposal-and I offer it humbly as coming from a junior member. If the government wishes to meet the problem there are two principal things which in my opinion it can do. First of all, it should endeavour at once to secure a joint inquiry, international in its scope, into the question. There are several ways in which that could be taken up. The British Board of Trade may be ridiculed by hon. members opposite as hope-

Tax Collections
less, but I venture to suggest that they would receive a friendly hearing. At least I should like to have their report after a real conference had been held. Again the government might take up the matter with the International Institute of Agriculture at Rome with a view to seeing what could be done or the government could take steps to bring about if possible an international conference under the League of Nations. So that there are several ways in which action might be taken. Secondly, I urge that in the meantime something be done, and I do think that the government should take some steps in the matter. What should those further steps be? There are two methods by which immediate relief might be brought to the present situation. One would be to amplify the present merchant marine service by adding to it ships constructed in Canada. The government could help the employment situation by building ships of its own. Why not capitalize this subsidy and issue bonds that would necessitate the payment of annual interest equal to $1,350,000, and so have enough money to build all the boats needed to augment the present Canadian Government Merchant Marine service and provide a really competitive force on the Atlantic? I offer that suggestion to the government. I understand that the capital so invested would provide about 21 new boats, efficient and up-to-date, instead of ten. But if the government does not want that, there is an abundance of empty tonnage on the market of the world anxiously awaiting a purchaser. Buy what tonnage may be needed and use it to control rates if you think you can break the combine that way. The second method is this: The government might take into consideration the possibility of getting the present Canadian Government Merchant Marine and the Canadian Pacific Railway boats to work in harmony in some attempt to create competition in Atlantic rates.
For the life of me I cannot understand how any government or any body of men can imagine that ten small boats, or even twelve or fifteen, of the tonnage specified in the agreement, can hope to make the least impression upon a combine of such an immense and powerful character nor affect rates unless those ten boats carry only a few commodities of a special kind at special rates. They can unquestionably establish competitive rates on the commodities which they carry in large enough quantities, but this would not be the case with other commodities. I regret therefore that unless the government can make some intimation, such as I suggested in the 8&i
earlier part of my remarks, and not press to a vote the second reading of the resolution, I shall be compelled to vote against the motion.

speechtext: Will the hon. member permit me to direct his attention to what I really did say on that occasion?

I do not
question the hon. member's intentions in the least. Possibly he did not mean what he said.
